They want cheaper electricity; they just oppose building the cheapest new electricity. They want a reliable grid; they just oppose the transmission needed to connect new generation. They want Australian manufacturing to grow; they just oppose the investment certainty manufacturers need. They want coal fired power stations to stay open; they just do not want to explain who is going to keep them running. Apparently, after doing all of that, power prices will magically fall! That is not an energy policy; it is a wish list with all the difficult bits crossed out. Governing requires more than announcing the destination. You have to explain how you are going to get there. Let's take coal. Those opposite talk about ageing coal fired power stations as if governments can simply order them to continue operating forever. But these are enormous pieces of industrial machinery. They wear out. Boilers deteriorate. Turbines require major

speaker: Tom French
heading: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS · Energy
text: overhauls. Maintenance costs increase. Eventually, the owners look at the cost of keeping those plants open and make a commercial decision. You cannot repeal metal fatigue. You cannot move an amendment to stop a boiler tube leaking, and you certainly cannot run a national electricity market on nostalgia. So when the coalition keep saying, 'Keep the old plants open,' there are some fairly obvious questions—for how long, at what cost, who pays and what will replace them eventually? These are not minor details. While those opposite were in government, 24 of Australia's 28 coal fired power stations brought forward their closure dates. Four gigawatts of dispatchable generation left the system and only one gigawatt went in. They knew these generators were going to close. The companies told them, the market told them and the engineers told them. Instead of building what came next, Australia got a decade of political warfare over energy. Then the bill arrived. They promised wholesale electricity prices below $70 a megawatt hour. They left government with

speaker: Tom French
heading: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS · Energy
text: wholesale prices above $280. Apparently their answer is now to do it all again—delay investment, oppose transmission, create uncertainty, keep ageing generators running longer and then act surprised when electricity becomes expensive. But this debate is not only about household power bills; it is about Australian industry. For decades, some of our biggest manufacturers have relied on long-term electricity contracts. Those contracts gave them certainty to invest, employ people and compete internationally. But those contracts won't last forever. Manufacturers are now looking at the next 10 or 20 years, and that is where energy policy stops being a political argument and becomes industrial policy. If we want to make things in Australia, we need abundant, reliable and internationally competitive electricity, not eventually; we need to build it now. That is why certainty matters. Generation matters. Storage matters. Transmission matters. Businesses need to know what that system looks like. Investors need to know what we are building, and workers need to know that those jobs have a future. The independent experts

speaker: Tom French
heading: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS · Energy
text: are remarkably consistent. The Australian Energy Market Operator says: Renewable energy, firmed with storage, backed up by gas and connected with upgraded networks remains the least-cost road map … The CSIRO says: Renewables supported by storage remain the lowest-cost generation investments … The Australian Energy Market Commission has warned that delaying generation, batteries and transmission risks higher electricity prices. So the choice is straightforward: with aging infrastructure that needs replacing, we can plan the replacement, attract investment and build it before the system disappears, or we can delay, pretend the old system will last forever and eventually discover that infrastructure does not care about political slogans. Labor is choosing to build more generation, more storage and more transmission, firming capacity and a system capable of supporting Australian industry for decades to come. Those opposite offer something different: cheap power without new generation, reliability without investment, manufacturing without certainty and aging power stations without the maintenance bill. There is a technical term for a policy like that—it doesn't work. The coalition spent a decade discovering that the hard way. Australia should not have to pay for them to learn it twice.

speaker: Andrew Willcox
heading: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS · Energy
text: Australia should be an energy superpower. We have coal and we have gas. We have the resources to power our nation; yet under this government, Australians are paying more for intermittent, unreliable power. Electricity bills have increased by around 40 per cent, and remember, this is after the Prime Minister said that under his leadership, power would be $245 cheaper. It looks like he's changed his position again. Over the past four years, Australian households have spent an extra $23 billion on energy bills. That's cold, hard cash being taken from family budgets—money that could have paid for groceries, school fees or mortgage repayments. Australians are experiencing a Labor created cost-of-living crisis and, under this Prime Minister, there's no sign of that ending. The result of high energy costs? Well, for small businesses, it means higher operating costs. For manufacturers, it means higher production costs. For farmers, it means higher costs to pump water, run machinery and keep their paddocks ploughed. For restaurants, it means higher costs to cook, cool

speaker: Andrew Willcox
heading: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS · Energy
text: and serve, which results in more expensive nights out for everyone. For transport operators, it means higher costs to keep the trucks moving. Energy is not some abstract policy debate; it's the engine of our economy. When energy prices rise, everything that uses energy becomes more expensive. When Australians pay more for power than they do overseas, we lose our competitive advantage. That means fewer opportunities for Australian workers and greater reliance on products made from somewhere else. We are already becoming dangerously dependent on fuel from overseas. Around 90 per cent of our transport fuel is now imported from overseas. We're relying on other countries to keep Australia moving. When the supply is disrupted, the shock travels fast. It hits the bowser, the farm gate and the family budget. For a country with all the resources, this is simply not good enough. Our economy depends on fuel. Higher transport costs mean higher costs for everyone. A country like Australia should never be caught short on energy. It is needed

speaker: Andrew Willcox
heading: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS · Energy
text: for our economy—to keep it moving. We need an energy policy that starts with what actually works, not what fits this Labor ideology. The coalition's plan is simple. We will use every reliable tool available to us—coal, gas, hydro and renewables, in the right place—and it's time to remove the ban on nuclear. This should not be a contest between technologies; it should be a contest to deliver better outcomes. If a technology can't provide affordable, reliable energy, we should not be prepared to use it. If it can strengthen our grid, support Australian industry and keep the lights on, then it deserves a place. We should not be shutting down proven energy sources before we have reliable replacements ready. We should not be asking Australian families to carry the cost of that experiment. The government talks constantly about the transition, but Australians are asking a much simpler question: when will the power become affordable again? You cannot build a stronger economy on ever-rising energy costs. You cannot create manufacturing

speaker: Andrew Willcox
heading: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS · Energy
text: jobs by making manufacturing more expensive. And you cannot claim to have energy security while importing nine out of every 10 litres of fuel. Australia does not have an energy shortage; Labor has an energy policy problem. We have the resources, we have the technology, we have the workers and we have the capability to power our future, but we need a government with the political will to use them. Australians need energy that is reliable and affordable. Businesses need certainty. Farmers need competitiveness. Manufacturers need lower input costs. Workers need secure jobs. And families need to know that, when the power bill arrives, they can afford to pay it. This government has made energy more expensive and less secure. The alternative is clear, and it starts with a cheaper, better, fairer plan: an energy system that puts Australian households and jobs first. Australia has the resources to be an energy superpower. The coalition has the plan to make it work for them. (Time expired)

speaker: Tracey Roberts
heading: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS · Energy
text: The incorporated speech read as follows— I totally oppose this motion. While it claims to address high energy costs, it ignores their structural causes and would leave Australians exposed to breakdowns, price spikes and higher bills. Australia's coal-fired power stations are ageing and increasingly unreliable. Of 28 coal plants, 24 brought their closure dates forward. Four gigawatts of dispatchable energy came off the grid, while only one gigawatt came on. The coalition promised wholesale electricity prices below $70 per megawatt hour. Instead, it left office with prices above $280. In May 2022, the average price was $341.25. The then energy minister changed the law to keep electricity price hikes secret ahead of the 2022 election. The coalition promised $1 billion to add 3,800 megawatts of electricity to the grid, yet three years later not one dollar nor one kilowatt had been delivered. The answer is rebuilding Australia's grid with low-cost renewable energy, backed by firming and upgraded networks. Since the Albanese government was elected in 2022, more than 22 gigawatts

speaker: Tracey Roberts
heading: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS · Energy
text: of wind and solar have been added to the grid. Wind and solar capacity has increased by 60 per cent—more than five times the capacity of the Snowy hydro schemes. Independent market bodies support this direction. The Australian Energy Market Operator says renewable energy, firmed with storage, backed by gas and connected through upgraded networks, remains the least-cost road map for Australia. The Australian Energy Regulator reports wholesale electricity spot prices have fallen since late 2022 because of lower fuel costs, increased renewable energy and government actions. CSIRO finds renewables supported by storage remain the lowest-cost generation investments for Australia's future electricity system. The Australian Energy Market Commission projects residential electricity per-unit prices will fall by around five per cent over the next five years, but it warns those prices risk rising 13 per cent from 2030 to 2035 unless renewable generation, batteries and transmission are delivered faster. Clean Energy Council research found household power bills could rise by $449 per year by 2030, with greater reliance on gas and

speaker: Tracey Roberts
heading: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS · Energy
text: coal and slower renewable construction. If a major coal-fired power plant also failed unexpectedly, that increase could reach $606. Yet the opposition proposes keeping ageing, unreliable coal generators operating longer. These plants can break down without warning, and those breakdowns cause price spikes. Their scheme would pour billions of taxpayer dollars into propping up ageing coal instead of building renewables backed by hydro, batteries and fast, flexible gas. During the coalition's decade in government, 24 of Australia's 28 coal-fired power stations announced they were closing. Four gigawatts of dispatchable energy came off the grid and only one gigawatt came on. Australians cannot afford to keep paying for that failure to prepare. Treasury modelling also warns that not pursuing net zero by 2050 risks lower economic growth, reduced investment, missed export and employment opportunities, and higher energy prices. It estimates a disorderly transition would cost the Australian economy $1.2 trillion between now and 2050. The Albanese Labor government's plan is renewables backed by gas, batteries and hydro. We have acted through

speaker: Tracey Roberts
heading: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS · Energy
text: power bill relief, gas price caps and investment in cheap renewables. We are also supporting households to electrify and install batteries. We are also fixing the retail electricity market to give consumers a fairer deal. New rules will prevent retailers increasing prices more than once a year, protect customers when low-cost offers expire, ban excessive charges such as late-payment fees, guarantee a fee-free payment method and require stronger assistance for vulnerable customers experiencing hardship. It is also about replacing ageing generation before it fails, rather than asking taxpayers and consumers to carry the cost of keeping unreliable coal plants operating beyond their planned lives. This motion misdiagnoses the causes of high electricity prices and offers policies that would make Australia's energy transition slower and more expensive. We should instead build the modern energy system Australians need: abundant renewable generation, firmed by batteries, hydro and flexible gas, connected by the transmission infrastructure required to deliver it. That is the least-cost roadmap identified by Australia's energy market operator. It lowers emissions, supports jobs and provides a pathway to a more reliable electricity system. I strongly urge the House to reject this misguided motion. Debate adjourned.

speaker: Alison Penfold
heading: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS · Tertiary Education and Training
text: is why Commonwealth payments are not simply student assistance; they are our regional workforce policy. While I welcome the expansion, we should also be clear the job is still not finished. There are allied health students undertaking substantial mandatory professional placements who remain outside the scheme. Nuclear medicine students are one example. The government has chosen 10 disciplines for this expansion, but nuclear medicine is not among them. That exposes a broader problem with drawing an arbitrary line through the allied health workforce. If we accept the principle that a student should not be financially punished because their professional qualification requires them to undertake weeks or months of mandatory unpaid placement, then that principle should be applied consistently. A nuclear medicine student loses their income while on placement, just as a radiography student does. They can face the same petrol costs, the same accommodation bill, the same rent waiting for them at home and the same pressure to choose between keeping a job and completing their degree. The financial hardship

speaker: Susan Templeman
heading: STATEMENTS BY MEMBERS · New South Wales: Storms
text: A fierce storm swept across Macquarie at the weekend, causing widespread fallen trees, branches and powerlines and requiring an immediate emergency response to clear roads and damaged homes. I know we were all grateful to the SES, RFS, police, fire and ambulance crews who turned out to assist, and to the Endeavour Energy and Telstra crews trying to do repairs. The Hawkesbury saw the worst of the power outages, with tens of thousands of homes blacked out into Sunday, which was particularly distressing for people relying on power for sewerage and water and for those facing the loss of perishables in homes and restaurants that were stocked up for Father's Day. Endeavour Energy returned about 60,000 homes across the region at the weekend, calling in assistance from another energy company. But, even today, they still have work to do to restore the remaining 1,400 customers as quickly and safely as possible. The most heavily impacted areas remain Mount Tomah, Bilpin and Colo, with significant damage along Bells Line of Road

speaker: Tony Pasin
heading: STATEMENTS BY MEMBERS · Energy
text: Energy bills for Australian businesses, families and industry, including in Barker, have skyrocketed by nearly 40 per cent. The Albanese Labor government promised power bills would fall by $275. Instead, nearly a quarter-of-a-million households have been forced onto hardship or payment assistance plans. Constituents in Barker have told me they can't afford to use the heater, have timed short showers and keep stove use to an absolute minimum. Australians are suffering because of this government's obsession with net zero, which has driven up the cost of power, destroyed manufacturing and gutted regional communities while doing nothing—I say nothing—to change the climate. We should be making the most of our abundant coal and gas to bring down the cost of energy, power industry and make Australian manufacturers, farmers and miners more competitive on the world stage. Labor's opposition to fossil fuels and their ideological obsession with renewables have meant resource projects have been buried under mountains of red, green and black tape. The coalition will scrap net zero and make Australia an energy superpower. We will use Australia's abundant energy resources, keep reliable generation in the system, lift the ban on nuclear power and unlock more Australian gas for Australians. Only the coalition has a strong plan to restore Australia's standard of living and protect our way of life.

speaker: Kara Cook
heading: MOTIONS · Cheaper Home Batteries Program
text: I move: That this House: (1) notes that: (a) 1 July 2026 marks one year since the Government launched the Cheaper Home Batteries Program, providing a discount of around 30 per cent on the cost of a typical home battery; and (b) in that time, more than 450,000 Australian households have installed a cheaper home battery; (2) commends the Government on one year of the Cheaper Home Batteries Program, which has delivered real cost of living relief to hundreds of thousands of Australian families and small businesses; (3) welcomes the Australian Energy Market Operator's findings last week that these batteries are already 'helping to moderate prices during evening peaks and to support grid reliability and security as coal plants withdraw'; and (4) supports the Government as it continues to make clean energy more affordable for all Australians. When I first tabled this motion, more than 450,000 cheaper home batteries had been installed right across Australia. Today that number has already passed 500,000. In just a matter of months, tens of

speaker: Kara Cook
heading: MOTIONS · Cheaper Home Batteries Program
text: thousands more Australian households, small businesses and community groups have taken up this program. And what does that say about this program? It says Australians want cheaper energy, they want more control over their power bills and, when we make clean-energy technology more affordable, Australians are ready to embrace it. I've seen this firsthand in my own community of Bonner. More than 4,300 cheaper home batteries have already been installed in Bonner, making us one of the leading electorates in Queensland for installations. Behind every one of those batteries is a household making a practical decision about how they can bring down their power bills and get more value from the solar energy they are already generating. Just over a year ago, the Albanese Labor government launched the Cheaper Home Batteries Program. The idea was pretty simple: we would help bring down the upfront cost of a typical home battery by around 30 per cent so more Australians could afford one. For many households it is a game changer, saving

speaker: Kara Cook
heading: MOTIONS · Cheaper Home Batteries Program
text: families $1,000 or more on their energy bills each and every year. Anyone who drives around my community knows just how many rooftop solar systems there are in Bonner. Across Brisbane's east and bayside, there are solar panels on roof after roof. Australians have already embraced the opportunity to generate their own cheap, clean energy. The next step is helping them keep more of it. A battery means the solar generated while you're at work or the kids are at school can be stored and used later. It is common sense and it is working. Those opposite like to suggest that programs like this are somehow just for wealthy people in the inner-city suburbs. The facts tell a very different story. More than three-quarters of the batteries installed through this program have been in outer suburban and regional communities. This is not an inner city story; this is a story about the suburbs and the regions right across our country. It is a story in communities like mine in the

speaker: Kara Cook
heading: MOTIONS · Cheaper Home Batteries Program
text: outer suburbs of Brisbane. The Australian Energy Market Operator has found that these batteries are already helping to moderate prices during evening peaks and support grid reliability and security as ageing coal-fired power stations withdraw. Labor's Cheaper Home Batteries Program is good for bills and good for the grid. We make better use of the enormous amount of solar Australia is already producing and we help bring down the costs of electricity at times when it is most expensive, so, even if you don't have a battery or even solar panels, you benefit from a stronger, more efficient energy system. Energy policy can sometimes seem complicated. We talk about generation, transmission, megawatts and wholesale markets, but for families in the community that I represent the question is much simpler: what does this mean for my power bill? Labor's plan is about more cheap, clean energy and a better deal for Australian households. So, when I look back at the motion that I submitted just a few months ago and see

speaker: Dan Tehan
heading: MOTIONS · Cheaper Home Batteries Program
text: I say respectfully to the member who's moved this motion that I hope that she has made sure that all the batteries in her electorate have been installed properly. I say this incredibly seriously because one of the things that this motion doesn't address is the way that this program has been rushed out. Already the reporting that we've seen, on the ABC and in newspapers, is about the potential risks of the rollout. That's why those of us on the opposition have called for an immediate audit of this program. There are two reasons why we need an immediate audit of this program. The first is around safety. This program was meant to cost the taxpayer around $2 billion. It's now in the budget forecasts that it's going to cost $8 billion. The money was rushing out the door so quickly that the department ran out of money to be able to fund it, so they had to go to the Clean Energy Regulator—who was meant to be overseeing

speaker: Dan Tehan
heading: MOTIONS · Cheaper Home Batteries Program
text: and supervising the scheme—to fund it. I can't ever remember where the regulator has been called in to finance a program—because the money's running out the door so quickly—because the department has actually run out of money. That should ring alarm bells to start with. What should ring alarm bells is that, every time we have quizzed the minister or sought documents from the minister about how the program's safety checks are going, we get nothing. We have to remember that one of the organisations which are doing the safety checks is the Smart Energy Council. People say, 'What would be wrong with the Smart Energy Council doing it?' Well, the problem with that would be that they actually fund the government. They pay money to the Labor Party for political campaigning, so how can they independently look at this program when they're a funder of the Labor Party? They pay donations to the Labor Party, and they're being asked to oversee this. So, when a program like 7.30 starts

speaker: Dan Tehan
heading: MOTIONS · Cheaper Home Batteries Program
text: asking serious questions around safety, I think it's time for an independent audit. When the Australian has on its front page a fellow who's had a battery installed, but because it's been stored in an area where the temperature drops and then rises, he's had to put a blanket on his battery, it's because he's worried about what the implications will be for the integrity of that battery. We can sit here and say, 'Oh, isn't this wonderful? We've been throwing money out the door—$2 billion to $8 billion,' but there's also got to be questions raised around whether the government is sure, then, that people haven't been abusing this. Does it have proper integrity? The last time we had a program that went from $2 billion to $8 billion—where the regulator had to fund it, where it looked like the government had no idea what it had embarked on—it was a scheme which, sadly, the government ended up having to pull in, and we ended up having a royal

speaker: Susan Templeman
heading: MOTIONS · Cheaper Home Batteries Program
text: Well, no wonder people think that the opposition's living in the Dark Ages. Let's be clear about what we inherited and why the program of renewables and batteries for households is so important. Under the previous mob, 24 out of 28 coal plants brought their closure dates forward, four gigawatts of dispatchable energy came off the grid and only one gigawatt came on. That's the legacy that those opposite left the country with because of their ideological opposition to the cheapest form of energy: renewables. They promised a wholesale energy price of $70 a megawatt hour. They left office with a wholesale energy price of over $280 per megawatt hour. That has caused ripple effects through Australian families, and we are working hard to make up for that. Instead of facing up to the Australian people and telling them that energy prices were going to go up, they changed the law so they didn't have to tell people. That's the legacy that they left. Yet in spite of that, we

speaker: Susan Templeman
heading: MOTIONS · Cheaper Home Batteries Program
text: have Australians now able to really embrace renewables. Not every Australian can access the Cheaper Home Batteries Program because it's home owners who can, so there is more work to do to ensure that this program and the benefits that are felt by it can be shared more widely. But let's think about this. Australia already has more than one in three homes with rooftop solar. People who like their gadgets tell me they love watching how much solar is being generated through their system when it's a nice sunny day. Now what the Cheaper Home Batteries Program does is help households store the solar energy that they generate during the day and use it when they need it most after the sun goes down. It's just commonsense. It's about putting families back in control of their energy bills, it's about helping households keep more of the cheap energy they generate themselves and it's working. In my electorate of Macquarie, we now have around 6,000 solar batteries across small businesses,

speaker: Susan Templeman
heading: MOTIONS · Cheaper Home Batteries Program
text: homes and community organisations, and that's introducing a massive 184,002 kilowatt hours in usable capacity in the grid. Basically one in 10 homes now in Macquarie have a battery to back up their solar. Across the Blue Mountains, Emu Plains, Leonay, Emu Heights and the Hawkesbury, we know that families are benefiting. It's a game changer for their energy bills, with many able to save up to $1,000 or even more off their energy bill each year. With those savings on bills, people will also be able to pay down the cost of their battery faster if they borrowed to do that. Batteries are good for bills and good for the grid because it means we're getting more cheap, fast, safe solar energy available in our homes, night or day, when and where it's needed. I know there were some people at the weekend who were very grateful they had installed a battery because, when the storm swept through and the power went down, for some families their battery was

speaker: Susan Templeman
heading: MOTIONS · Cheaper Home Batteries Program
text: able to kick in and keep their lights on until power was restored. The Cheaper Home Batteries Program is bringing down the cost of a typical battery by about 30 per cent—you save about a third—and, because of our responsible budget management, more Australians can actually take up the discount. Every battery installed means another household is getting more value from their rooftop solar, and it's another job for local installers and small businesses who are delivering this rollout across the country. I'm really proud to have spent time with businesses like Blue Mountains Solar and PSC Energy, who used to be called Penrith Solar Centre—it's how some people who've been around for a while might know them. These are organisations that care about the work they do. They're doing it with integrity. They are great for giving advice about what's best for your home. There are many others like them across our community—local businesses who take pride in their work. Even if you don't have a battery, there are benefits for the whole community, because these home batteries mean there's less pressure on the grid at peak times and lower reliance on expensive generation, and that means downward prices for everybody. So it's a win-win.

speaker: Nicolette Boele
heading: MOTIONS · Cheaper Home Batteries Program
text: I welcome the motion from the member for Bonner. The government doesn't get everything right, but they've done a fantastic job with the Cheaper Home Batteries Program. I called for a home battery subsidy in the lead-up to the last election, and I was delighted when the government committed to a 30 per cent subsidy for households. The response was massive. Uptake rapidly outpaced expectations, with over 1,000 batteries being installed every single day. This is world-leading stuff—truly astonishing figures. In the last financial year, nearly 60 per cent of household-scale batteries across every country in the world, except for China, were installed right here in Australia. We crossed the 500,000 home battery mark last month. With batteries all the old arguments against renewables—that wind and solar are unreliable and need lots of expensive gas backups—just fall away. Batteries make the grid more stable. They make households energy independent, and they cut power bills. Australia's benchmark electricity price fell by up to 10 per cent a few months ago, specifically

speaker: Nicolette Boele
heading: MOTIONS · Cheaper Home Batteries Program
text: because battery storage was displacing the need for expensive gas peaking. One of my constituents shared her battery story with me recently. When she moved into a 1970s home in Gordon last year with poor insulation, her household electricity bill jumped to $525 in one month—ouch. Fearing a $6,000 annual bill, her household installed solar panels and a 32-kilowatt-hour battery, making use of the 30 per cent subsidy. Well, their bills dropped to an average of $126 per month in winter and $40 a month in summer. That's a huge, huge difference in power bills, and they're expecting to recoup the costs in only 4½ years. She tells me that she 'couldn't be happier' and she says, 'It's a great feeling every day, to feel more self-sufficient and to know that we can live more comfortably with less stress.' With this subsidy, Australia has seized the global battery revolution with both hands, making the most of falling prices, improved safety standards and better resource efficiency to accelerate the rollout that

speaker: Nicolette Boele
heading: MOTIONS · Cheaper Home Batteries Program
text: we need to power our economy this century. The rapid uptake shows that Australians have an appetite for electrification. They love this stuff. We see it again and again. Electrification schemes, when they exist and they're well communicated, are more successful than anyone imagined. We saw it in the early days of the feed-in tariffs for rooftop solar, which kicked off what now sees Australia as the largest per capita solar user in the world. We saw it also with the discount on new EVs, which was more expensive than Treasury had anticipated because it was so popular. Now, beating expectations like this is not a sign of failure. It's a clear sign of success. The government should heed these findings and keep creating such schemes. It recently announced the extension of the solar scheme for households to be available to farmers, community facility managers and business owners so that they too can install solar systems. This is excellent news because it tackles what people call the missing middle of

speaker: Nicolette Boele
heading: MOTIONS · Cheaper Home Batteries Program
text: electrification. Solar panels can now go on factories, warehouses, farm sheds, dairies and other industrial buildings. Those enormous empty roofs could be covered in solar panels, and this scheme update will help make that happen. The next step is to ensure that renters and people living in apartments can also benefit from electrification. One important option is to make plug-in solar panels legal. You could just buy these simple appliances off the shelves at Bunnings, chuck them on your balcony or in your backyard, plug them in and save Aussies up to $370 a year on energy bills. They're legal in the UK, Germany, Spain and other countries. It's an easy win, just sitting on the shelves at Bunnings. If the huge success of the Cheaper Home Batteries Program is anything to go by, the government shouldn't waste any more time waiting.

speaker: Cassandra Fernando
heading: MOTIONS · Cheaper Home Batteries Program
text: Good policies are the ones people see working in their homes and feel in their household budgets. The Cheaper Home Batteries Program is exactly that kind of policy. Since 1 July last year, the Albanese Labor government's Cheaper Home Batteries Program has delivered more than 500,000 batteries for households, small businesses and community groups by cutting the upfront cost of a typical battery by around 30 per cent. Households with rooftop solar are saving up to $1,100 every year. It is extra room in a family budget when every dollar counts. More than one in three Australian homes have rooftop solar panels to generate cheap power during the day, but families need that power the most after sunset. A battery bridges that gap, storing energy so it is ready for dinner time, homework time and the evening peak. The equation is simple. Generate it during the day, store it, use it at night and pay less. Families in my electorate of Holt already understand this. There have been 3,729 solar

speaker: Cassandra Fernando
heading: MOTIONS · Cheaper Home Batteries Program
text: batteries installed in Holt, providing over 116,000 kilowatt hours of usable capacity. From Hampton Park to Narre Warren South all the way down to Cranbourne and Clyde North, households are taking control of the power they produce and the bills they pay. But batteries do more than lower individual household bills. When the Australian Energy Market Operator compared 10,000 homes with solar and batteries against 10,000 homes with solar alone, during the evening peak, homes with batteries drew 73 per cent less electricity from the grid. Let that sink in—73 per cent. That means less strain when the system is at its busiest, guaranteeing better reliability and putting downward pressure on power prices for everyone. That tells us that more than three-quarters of these installations are happening outside inner-city communities. Holt families aren't interested in ideological energy wars. They just want to know: If a policy works in practical terms, does it lower bills? Does it keep the lights on? On both tests, this program delivers. It helps households squeeze

speaker: Cassandra Fernando
heading: MOTIONS · Cheaper Home Batteries Program
text: every drop of value from solar panels that they've already paid for, all while supporting thousands of jobs for electricians, apprentices and small businesses across our suburbs and regions. Those opposite might talk this down, but let's be clear: a program delivering half a million batteries is not a disaster. A program cutting bills and stabilising the grid is not a disaster. A program that has doubled its installer workforce is not a disaster. It is delivery. The experts agree. Both AEMO and the CSIRO confirmed that renewable energy backed by storage is the lowest cost way to replace ageing coal and build the reliable grid Australia needs. What is the coalition's alternative? Is it to spend billions keeping old coal stations alive and pursuing nuclear reactors that would take years to build? We haven't forgotten their record. During their decade in office, 24 out of 28 coal plants announced closures, and, when benchmark power prices were set to surge just before the 2022 elections, they deliberately hid that fact

speaker: Cassandra Fernando
heading: MOTIONS · Cheaper Home Batteries Program
text: from the Australian people until after polling day. The choice today is clear. The coalition wants to freeze this progress and strip away household support. The Albanese Labor government is helping families lower their bills right now by backing local jobs and building a stronger, cheaper grid for the future. It is good for households, it is good for the grid and it is good for Holt homes.

speaker: Monique Ryan
heading: MOTIONS · Cheaper Home Batteries Program
text: I commend the government for the Cheaper Home Batteries Program. More than a year ago, the government provided Australian households, small businesses and community organisations with a discount of about 30 per cent on eligible battery storage systems. Those batteries allow for storage of abundant cheap solar energy generated during the day for use at a time when electricity is more expensive. There have been more than 500,000 battery installations since the program started, reflecting the enormous scale of household demand when the economics stack up. The member for Bonner is right. Australia's energy transition is delivering real savings. However, at the moment these savings are generally flowing in the direction of those who are in a position to access the energy transition. Renters, apartment dwellers and people living in other forms of multioccupancy housing are locked out of the scheme, which requires pairing a battery with rooftop solar on a property that the applicant can modify. Vulnerable households, low-income households and renters are still missing out. Around one-third of

speaker: Monique Ryan
heading: MOTIONS · Cheaper Home Batteries Program
text: Australians rent, and they're more likely to experience energy hardship than home owners. But only 11 per cent of rentals have solar, compared to 44 per cent of home owners, and only six per cent of apartments, compared to 39 per cent of detached or semidetached homes. So for too many people the possibility of accessing free electricity harvested from the sun hitting their roof is at the whim of a landlord with little financial incentive to invest in solar and storage. This is a gap that the Commonwealth should help close, working with the states, and I call on the government to consider more reforms to facilitate household electrification. Firstly, the government should, and could, expand direct Commonwealth finance and incentives, like the Household Energy Upgrades Fund, so that landlords have a genuine incentive to install solar, batteries and energy efficient appliances in rental properties. Secondly, we should work to make portable plug-in solar panels legal to install and use in Australian homes. Small standalone solar units attached to

speaker: Monique Ryan
heading: MOTIONS · Cheaper Home Batteries Program
text: balconies or used in backyards and plugged into power points can produce enough power to run a fridge, a television and other appliances during the day. They're already legal in the UK, in Germany, in Spain and in New Zealand; they should be legal here too. Researchers have estimated that Australians living in capital cities could save between $226 and $372 every year with a plug-in solar system. A kit that costs about $1,000 would pay for itself in three years and would keep working for 20 years. And renters could take it with them when they move. Thirdly, the government should adjust tax policy settings to reward landlords who bring their properties up to a high energy performance standard. And, finally, the government should work with the states towards a national target for rental homes to be fully electrified by 2040. The states are already showing what is possible when there is a clear road map. Victoria's Gas Substitution Roadmap sets out that, from 1 January 2027, all new

speaker: Monique Ryan
heading: MOTIONS · Cheaper Home Batteries Program
text: homes and commercial buildings will be built all electric, while new minimum energy efficiency standards for rental properties will come into force shortly after that. The ACT has also committed to phasing out fossil gas entirely by 2045. These approaches are encouraging, but they highlight the need for national coordination and direction. The Cheaper Home Batteries Program has proven that when the Commonwealth gets the settings right, Australians will respond. We are now a world leader in rooftop solar, but the benefits of rooftop renewables are unevenly and inequitably distributed. Too many of the 2.5 million Australians who live in apartments or units are still missing out. Let's make sure that the benefits of cheap electricity from renewables extend to every Australian home, not just to those people who are currently lucky enough to own the roof over their heads.

speaker: Tom Venning
heading: MOTIONS · Taxation
text: Treasurer who believes chocolate milk comes from brown cows bought a farm with your money. The Commonwealth, using your taxes, chipped in $69 million, plus another $8.8 million for the trees. Australian farmers were outbid with their own taxes. speaker: Sophie Scamps
heading: CONSTITUENCY STATEMENTS · Climate Change, Human Rights
text: I rise to express my deepest condolences to the Tibetan and Nepalese communities following the devastating floods in Nepal and Tibet and the tragic loss of life they have caused. I know the ramifications of this disaster are being deeply felt by Tibetan and Nepalese communities around the world, including families in my electorate of Mackellar. I thank the Australian government for providing support to affected communities in Nepal, and I know that trying to locate people still missing, including Australians, is the priority. But, as we navigate the aftermath of this disaster, it is vital that we understand the context of what has led to this. Tibet is on the front line of global climate change. The glaciers of the Tibetan Plateau known as the Third Pole are especially vulnerable to a warming climate, increasing the risk of sudden and catastrophic flooding. Tibet is a country that is under occupation by China. Tibetans are denied the right to steward their rivers and natural resources. For years, Tibetans have warned

speaker: Susan Templeman
heading: STATEMENTS ON INDULGENCE · Himalayas: Floods
text: what history tells us happens. Plan has been looking at this situation across disasters for many, many, many years. Nepal is the 20th-most disaster-prone country in the world, with frequent floods, riverbank erosion and landslides—all major climate related hazards. As they say, this flood didn't create the link between climate change and girls' future in Nepal, but it accelerates a trend that Plan International has already documented and qualified. In 2023 their research found that, in Nepal, students are on average losing three months of their education every year due to climate disasters. The same research found that a third of young people surveyed said their schools had been closed, damaged or destroyed by climate related events in the past year, and almost half felt unsafe travelling to and from school because of climate related disasters. This is a really profound effect already, and the disaster that we've seen clearly is on much bigger scale. The thing we need to be mindful of as we provide aid to Nepal is

speaker: Monique Ryan
heading: STATEMENTS ON INDULGENCE · Himalayas: Floods
text: Scientists have been clear that the glacial lake which collapsed had shown visible signs of instability in the days beforehand and that outburst floods of this kind are becoming more frequent as the Himalayan glaciers retreat under a warming climate. Nepal's foreign minister has called on the international community to treat this as a climate event, not a freak accident. He's right to do so. The Hindu Kush Himalayan region holds the largest volume of ice outside the polar regions, and it's warming faster than the global average. Every fraction of a degree of warming that we fail to prevent increases the risk of another such event. Nepalese community members present in Kooyong on Sunday asked for our assistance in highlighting how global warming acts as a critical risk multiplier in Nepal's valleys, increasing the risk of flash flooding driven by accelerated glacier melt. They made the point that, as a wealthy middle power with abundant renewable resources, Australia does have a regional influence and a responsibility to lead. By

speaker: Monique Ryan
heading: STATEMENTS ON INDULGENCE · Himalayas: Floods
text: rapidly decoupling our own economy from fossil fuels, we don't just reduce our own emissions. We can demonstrate that a low-carbon economy is practical and achievable, and we can set a standard for global action to protect vulnerable communities. We can't personally rebuild the homes or return the lives lost in Nepal and Tibet, but we can honour them by taking seriously our own responsibility to cut emissions, to support our Pacific and South Asian neighbours in their climate adaptation and to treat the accelerating instability of glaciers and ice sheets as the urgent global security issue that it now is. I extend my condolences and those of the Kooyong community to everyone who has lost something in this disaster, and I commit to continuing to press this parliament to act on the climate change that's making tragedies like this more common and more severe.

speaker: Anne Webster
heading: STATEMENTS BY MEMBERS · Climate Change
text: In 1949, I say for all the students here—welcome—George Orwell wrote his dystopian novel 1984 , a book designed to warn people about the dangers of government overreach and control after World War II. speaker: Dan Tehan
heading: QUESTIONS WITHOUT NOTICE · Cheaper Home Batteries Program
text: My question is to the Minister for Climate Change and Energy. Can the minister guarantee that all batteries installed under the government's Cheaper Home Batteries Program have been installed safely and in compliance with technical requirements?

speaker: Chris Eyles Bowen
heading: QUESTIONS WITHOUT NOTICE · Cheaper Home Batteries Program
text: I thank the honourable member for the question. What I can guarantee is that every single cheaper home battery has been installed under the Small-scale Renewable Energy Scheme, which is one of the world's most rigorous schemes for compliance, which has been operating under governments of both persuasions and ministers of both persuasions and has ensured the safe rollout of more than four million rooftop solar installations and more than half a million cheaper home battery installations. The member refers to complaints about cheaper home batteries. I can confirm that this scheme has received 315 complaints in relation to the Small-scale Renewable Energy Scheme, which covers solar panel installations, battery installations and solar hot water installations. That is 0.04 per cent of 800,000 installations in the last 12 months. Of those complaints, 106 matters were referred for other enforcement and 17 matters have needed to be progressed for formal investigations. That's 17 out of more than 530,000 cheaper home battery installations and 800,000 others. That's 0.002 per cent of installed systems referred for formal investigation and 0.01 per cent referred to other enforcement agencies.

speaker: Dan Tehan
heading: QUESTIONS WITHOUT NOTICE · Cheaper Home Batteries Program

speaker: Milton Dick

speaker: Chris Eyles Bowen
heading: QUESTIONS WITHOUT NOTICE · Cheaper Home Batteries Program

I've got to say these are highly credentialed, well-qualified, hardworking Australians, and they do not need to be traduced by the member for Wannon or anyone else. I don't

speaker: Chris Eyles Bowen

They have halved. Complaints per thousand installations have halved since this came in. Again, I say to those opposite: 535,833 Australian houses have installed a cheaper home battery. I know they don't like it—

speaker: Chris Eyles Bowen

speaker: Tania Lawrence
heading: ADJOURNMENT · Tertiary Education and Training, Energy, Workplace Relations
text: One thing I've said many times in this place is that talent is spread everywhere across this great nation but opportunities are not. We are absolutely working and are determined to change that, and we can see that in our evidence with our investment into skills. It's why we introduced fee-free TAFE and why now more than 850,000 Australians have enrolled in training that can change the trajectory of their lives, and it's why I was proud to see the Albanese and Cook Labor governments come together to invest $32 million in the new Clean Energy Skill Hub at Midland TAFE, right in the heart of my electorate of Hasluck. This investment will help train the next generation of electricians, instrumentation technicians, engineers and skilled tradespeople who will be powering Australia's economic future. It means more opportunities closer to home, it means local people being able to access world-class training without having to leave their community, and it means ensuring Western Australians have the skills required to take advantage of

speaker: Tania Lawrence
heading: ADJOURNMENT · Tertiary Education and Training, Energy, Workplace Relations
text: the opportunities being created by Australia's energy transformation. As the Minister for Climate Change and Energy has observed, the global shift to clean energy represents one of the biggest economic transformations since the Industrial Revolution, and it presents Australia with an enormous economic and jobs opportunity. I believe that opportunity should belong to Australian workers. The Clean Energy Skill Hub is a practical example of what good government looks like. Federal Labor and WA Labor are working together to ensure that, as industries evolve and new technologies emerge, local workers have the skills and qualifications they need to succeed. It's an investment in people, an investment in productivity and an investment in the long-term future of Western Australia. But there has to be a pathway from training to employment. If governments are investing in skills and workers are doing the training, industry also has a responsibility to ensure qualified Australians have a genuine opportunity to apply for the jobs that are being created. Whether we're talking about offshore oil and

speaker: Tania Lawrence
heading: ADJOURNMENT · Tertiary Education and Training, Energy, Workplace Relations
text: gas, critical minerals, maritime operations or emerging clean energy projects, Western Australians rightly expect that, when they have the qualifications, experience and willingness to work, they will have a fair chance to secure those jobs. That is why I've been listening carefully to the concerns being raised by the Offshore Alliance, which represents thousands of workers across Western Australia. Their members have voiced concerns that qualified Australian workers are sometimes being overlooked, while employers increasingly rely on temporary visa arrangements. Their message is straightforward: where Australians are qualified, ready and available to do the work, they deserve a genuine opportunity to apply for those jobs first. I support that principle. This is not about closing Australia off from the world. Australia will always benefit from skilled migration and international expertise, but Australian workers should be able to expect a fair return from the industries that rely on Australia's resources, Australia's infrastructure and Australia's communities. The same principle applies in another industry that keeps our economy moving every day—transport. Tomorrow, thousands

speaker: Tom Venning
heading: CONSTITUENCY STATEMENTS · Sport, Energy
text: 45 electorates were never invited to apply—including in my electorate of Grey, which has 30 local government areas and spans a landmass bigger than the state of New South Wales. speaker: Zali Steggall
heading: STATEMENTS ON INDULGENCE · Himalayas: Floods
text: ice and massive movements from glaciers, particularly in Chamonix in the French Alps. It is staggering when it happens. The noise, the volume and impact is just really hard to describe. So I think we really have to have this conversation around monitoring, measuring and acknowledging how much our warming climate is going to put so many communities at risk that may find themselves in valleys such as this. We can't yet quantify how much climate change contributed to this particular tragedy, but we can say with absolute certainty that continued warming increases dangerous instability in high mountain environments and that communities need much stronger protection. The growing danger is a consequence of decades of inadequate action. Every delay in cutting pollution allows more warming to continue and makes the task of keeping people safe harder. The ultimate tragedy of this, in particular, is that those who have contributed the least to warming through emissions are the ones paying the highest price. By continually downplaying risks, governments are failing to

speaker: Zali Steggall
heading: STATEMENTS ON INDULGENCE · Himalayas: Floods
text: invest in adaptation and preparedness and leaving communities exposed. In Warringah, we know climate risk reaches into people's homes and household budgets. Flood exposure and unaffordable insurance already affect our community. I've repeatedly called for greater investment in prevention and resilience and for polluters to contribute to the cost. That responsibility extends beyond our borders. Communities such as in Nepal and Tibet and our Pacific island neighbours, communities with the fewest resources to prepare for climate impacts and risks, should not be left to deal with the tragic consequences when disasters strike. Nepal's foreign minister, Shisir Khanal, has called for climate compensation. As he said, 'We have contributed so little to climate change.' He called on those benefiting from larger, more polluting economies to accept a shared responsibility. I agree. Australia should support that call, and we should apply the same principle to coal, oil and gas corporations who make obscene profits at the same time their products contribute to the warming that puts vulnerable communities at risk. It's time

speaker: Zali Steggall
heading: STATEMENTS ON INDULGENCE · Himalayas: Floods
text: to make polluters pay and hold them responsible for the damage they are causing. First, Australia should make a new climate finance pledge in line with our global fair share. We are heading into COP, and so there is a responsibility on Minister Bowen as president of the COP and on Australia as a major contributor through fossil fuel exports to global warming. That climate finance pledge should reflect our capacity to contribute and our responsibility for pollution with a clear timetable and transparent reporting on delivery, particularly as Australia is the 15th highest fossil fuel contributor per capita. That funding should be additional to existing development assistance. Helping people recover from climate damage must not come at the expense of their access to health care, education or food security. Second, we should prioritise international funds supporting low-income and climate-vulnerable countries like Nepal, including the Fund for responding to Loss and Damage and the Adaptation Fund. We need support for recovery alongside investment that helps prevent the next tragedy. That

speaker: Zali Steggall
heading: STATEMENTS ON INDULGENCE · Himalayas: Floods
text: means grants accessible to affected communities supporting early warning systems, safer infrastructure and locally led recovery. Countries already carrying the costs of climate change should not be pushed further into debt to rebuild after disaster. Third, Australia should establish a climate pollution levy on coal, oil and gas corporations operating here, with revenue paid into a dedicated climate compensation fund. The fund should provide a reliable contribution to climate recovery, including international loss and damage support for vulnerable countries. It should have independent oversight, public reporting and meaningful involvement from the communities it serves. Fourth, Australia should advocate internationally for other countries to introduce equivalent levies. It is time to step up and lean into leadership. It's not enough to show up and say you care if your actions don't match that stated care. We should use our diplomacy, including at climate negotiations and the G20, to build support for making fossil fuel producers contribute to climate compensations for countries like Nepal who are paying the price. Compensation, of course,

speaker: Jerome Laxale
heading: STATEMENTS ON INDULGENCE · Himalayas: Floods

heading: BILLS · Private Health Insurance Amendment (Modernising the Private Health Insurance Rebate) Bill 2026; Second Reading
