Where are we going to get the money from? They

speaker: David Farley
heading: STATEMENTS BY MEMBERS · Climate Change: Forestry Industry
text: Australians are being sold a new, improved $1.5 billion native forest fraud. That figure comes from government funded modelling from Mandala Partners, modelling that has never been released. The method was only registered on 26 June this year, yet the numbers behind it were locked in months earlier. Dr Raison, former CSIRO chief scientist, says the claim of 1.5 million credits a year is 60 per cent more carbon than exists in all the native timber felled in New South Wales annually. Forestry Australia says the method could overcredit by up to 100 per cent. The carbon price it relies on, $67 per unit, is 70 per cent above today's market. Strip away those fantasy numbers, and the real return is closer to $58 million. Research shows that 80 per cent of the timber we stop producing gets replaced by imports, much of it from high-risk, illegally logged sources. We're exporting our emissions, our standards, while claiming credit at home. Meanwhile, 8,900 jobs and a $2.9 billion industry are on the line, funded by a scheme that covers 15 years against a 100-year obligation. Before senators vote on 15 September, release the modelling and answer the experts. Australia deserves truth not fantasy.

speaker: Colin Boyce
heading: STATEMENTS BY MEMBERS · Gladstone Power Station
text: For nearly 50 years, Gladstone Power Station has provided affordable, reliable energy that powers our economy, supports families in the local community and keeps our major industries operating. This week we see that the Net Zero Economy Authority has begun consulting Gladstone workers and the community about what happens when the power station closes. Let me be very clear about what this means. The consultation is about managing the impacts of a closure that could happen six years before the station's planned retirement. Only weeks ago, Gladstone unit 2 underwent a multimillion-dollar shutdown and overhaul. This is a power station that is still maintained and invested in to operate, not an asset that has simply reached the end of its useful life. Yet, while workers are still overhauling the machinery that keeps Gladstone operating, the Net Zero Economy Authority has arrived in Gladstone to consult on what happens when it closes. Supplying around 80 per cent of its electricity directly to the local heavy industry, the Gladstone Power Station should

speaker: Colin Boyce
heading: STATEMENTS BY MEMBERS · Gladstone Power Station
text: remain operating until there is a reliable alternative with genuine certainty for industries and workers who depend on it. If coal is good enough to power other countries, it should be good enough to power Australia. That is why the coalition is committed to scrapping Labor's ideological net zero mandates and putting affordable, reliable energy and Australian jobs first—because regional Australians deserve better than a government that plans to close all of our industries.

speaker: Lisa Chesters
heading: QUESTIONS WITHOUT NOTICE · Energy
text: My question is to the Minister for Resources. How is the Albanese Labor government ensuring that more Australian gas is available for Australian households, businesses and industry at affordable prices whilst creating jobs, growing the economy and providing the energy security needed to support Australia's transition to net zero? Why is this needed after a decade of neglect?

speaker: Madeleine King
heading: QUESTIONS WITHOUT NOTICE · Energy
text: I thank the member for Bendigo for that question. She is a champion of her community. Today, this government, under the leadership of this Prime Minister, released the exposure draft legislation of the landmark Labor reform, the national gas reservation scheme. We are securing more Australian gas for Australian households, for Australian businesses, for Australian industry and for Australia's economic and energy security. For the member for Bendigo, and for members right around this country, this will drive thousands of new jobs in manufacturing and in the resources sector. It is gas in our reservation scheme that will allow the Fosterville and the Costerfield mines to employ more workers. I was lucky to visit the Fosterville mine, the great gold mine in the member for Bendigo's electorate, last year, and gas from that reservation will supply a diverse manufacturing base in Bendigo for products like ham and custard to the legendary Bushmaster vehicle, which is so essential for our defence forces. Australian consumers deserve and expect that they will be

speaker: Madeleine King
heading: QUESTIONS WITHOUT NOTICE · Energy
text: able to access affordable Australian gas before it heads overseas. This government will make that happen. What we are requiring of the gas industry is simple and it is fair. Simply set aside a portion of what you export for Australia, the nation that produces the product, and for the workers that have built the industry over decades. The rest of that gas? Well, that is open for export, and those exports will continue to provide for the energy security of our important trading partners. I'm asked about why this is needed after a wasted decade. In 2022 we inherited a gas policy bin fire from the coalition—a bin fire to say the least. Those opposite left this country ill prepared for the energy crisis that engulfed most of the world following Russia's invasion of Ukraine and ill prepared for the failure of coal-fired power plants that drove up gas prices and power prices to unacceptable levels. Since then, we have done much reform, and it has ended most recently

speaker: Madeleine King
heading: QUESTIONS WITHOUT NOTICE · Energy
text: with the gas market review that led to the conclusion that we need to build a national gas reservation scheme. The release of the exposure draft today is a major step forward, and I look forward to further consultation on this with industry and with the community and to working with parliament to achieve this energy and fuel security for Australians. It will be a matter for each member of the Liberal Party, for each member of the Nationals, for each member of One Nation and for others in this House and to decide if they want to support a gas reservation scheme that will deliver Australian gas for Australian households and Australian businesses. This government is committed to delivering Australian gas for Australians for the long-term future of this— (Time expired)

speaker: Pat Conroy
heading: QUESTIONS WITHOUT NOTICE · Fuel Security
text: I thank the member for Hunter, a staunch advocate for Aussie manufacturing if I've ever seen one. This gas reservation policy is a landmark Labor reform. Australia is a global energy and resources superpower, but, for too long, we've not value added these resources to create jobs and industries here. Australians expect us to do better, and that's why this policy is so important. Requiring gas exporters to reserve up to 20 per cent of their exports will ensure that our domestic gas market is always modestly oversupplied, securing the gas we need and pushing down prices for households and industry. We know that, when it comes to supporting industry and jobs, energy prices are critical. That's why we're using Australia's resources to power Aussie jobs, manufacturing, and long-term economic security and resilience. Australia has always been a country that makes things. For generations, workers in our factories, smelters, refineries and workshops helped build this country, but, unfortunately, under a wasted decade of the Liberal government, Australians were told it

speaker: Pat Conroy
heading: QUESTIONS WITHOUT NOTICE · Fuel Security
text: didn't matter if we made things here. They drove the car industry to leave, they oversaw the closure of three oil refineries, and they shut down two naval shipyards. They saw communities devastated, and they refuse to fight for those communities and those jobs. They did not care. Beyond the human toll, this undermined our national sovereignty and our resilience. During the pandemic, we didn't have all that we needed. When prices spiked during global conflict, we felt it. When supply chains seized, businesses wore the cost. We learnt that countries are stronger when they can make more things themselves, and we know that Australia has the workers, the resources, the energy and the ideas to build industries here, and we have a plan that is delivering. Today's announcement is all about supporting them. Aussie gas should go to Aussie industry and households first, and that's what our gas reservation policy does by requiring an oversupply. Our changes will mean manufacturers will access reliable and affordable energy they need to

speaker: Pat Conroy
heading: QUESTIONS WITHOUT NOTICE · Fuel Security
text: invest, produce and grow. Cheaper gas will help manufacturers remain globally competitive. We are a global energy and resources superpower, and a gas reservation policy helps us play to our strengths. These reforms put Australian gas users and Aussie workers first. Aussie resources are being used by Aussie manufacturers to make a future here under this prime minister.

speaker: Mr Tony Stephen Burke
heading: BUSINESS · Suspension of Standing and Sessional Orders
text: I move: That: (1) standing orders 31 and 33 be suspended for the remainder of the sitting; and (2) so much of the standing and sessional orders be suspended as would prevent: (a) private Members' business notice No. 11, relating to the disallowance of the Carbon Credits (Carbon Farming Initiative—Improved Forest Management in Multiple-Use Public Native Forests) Methodology Determination 2026 made under the Carbon Credits (Carbon Farming Initiative) Act 2011 on 25 June 2026 and presented to the House on 29 June 2026, standing in the name of the Member for Wannon, being called on and considered, with the total time for debate on the motion being no more than 40 minutes; (b) the House then considering any messages from the Senate; (c) Government business having priority until 4.30 pm; and (d) any variation to this arrangement being made only on a motion moved by a Minister.

speaker: Dan Tehan
heading: REGULATIONS AND DETERMINATIONS · Carbon Credits (Carbon Farming Initiative-Improved Forest Management in Multiple-use Public Native Forests) Methodology Determination 2026; Disallowance
text: I move: That the Carbon Credits (Carbon Farming Initiative-Improved Forest Management in Multiple-use Public Native Forests) Methodology Determination 2026 made under the Carbon Credits (Carbon Farming Initiative) Act 2011 on 25 June 2026 and presented to the House on 29 June 2026, be disallowed. This is a very simple motion. It seeks to prevent the federal and state Labor governments from stopping the destruction of native forestry industry on the altar of net zero. This is about jobs. This is about timber industry jobs and how the government wants to absolutely destroy them. And the worst thing is, they want to do it without being upfront about it. This is another sneaky way of hurting jobs in this nation, and especially jobs in rural and regional Australia. It has to stop. What have you got against regional and rural Australia? What have you got against timber worker jobs? We need these timber worker jobs. We need them. And not only that, we need the timber because the timber is sustainably

speaker: Dan Tehan
heading: REGULATIONS AND DETERMINATIONS · Carbon Credits (Carbon Farming Initiative-Improved Forest Management in Multiple-use Public Native Forests) Methodology Determination 2026; Disallowance
text: harvested in this country. And do you know what happens when you close it down here? It all gets imported. And where does it get imported from? Those countries that don't sustainably harvest. That is what is occurring here, and the government should be up front about it. That is why we have moved this disallowance motion. Enough with your pretence of trying to get to net zero. All you're doing is killing jobs and industry in this nation time after time after time after time, and we are going to oppose it every single step of the way. The regulation, which was authorised by the member for Fremantle on 25 June 2026, allows state governments to cash in climate credits for forestry they have saved. So let's put what they've done into real language: when you lock up the timber industry, you're going to allow state governments to get the carbon credits from it. That's what you've done. Basically, the minister sitting here at the table, the Minister for

speaker: Dan Tehan
heading: REGULATIONS AND DETERMINATIONS · Carbon Credits (Carbon Farming Initiative-Improved Forest Management in Multiple-use Public Native Forests) Methodology Determination 2026; Disallowance
text: Climate Change and Energy, cannot meet his targets, will not meet his targets, but is quite happy to target timber workers for his net zero approach. That is what this is about. We will not stand here and allow this to happen. The interesting thing about this is that we know that this is what this is all about, because the New South Wales state Labor government are the ones who've asked for it, with their Great Koala National Park—which they can't afford to pay for. We know this is going to lead to noxious weeds and feral animals in the farms adjacent to this state forest because the government will not finance and they will not fund the state parks around it. This is junk credit costing timber industry jobs. We will not sit here and allow it to happen. If allowed to stand, the new regulation would see the cessation of commercial timber harvesting across entire regional forest agreement areas. These areas were negotiated in good faith so

speaker: Dan Tehan
heading: REGULATIONS AND DETERMINATIONS · Carbon Credits (Carbon Farming Initiative-Improved Forest Management in Multiple-use Public Native Forests) Methodology Determination 2026; Disallowance
text: that timber jobs could stay in Australia. And yet this sneaky, underhanded way just seeks to undermine these agreements. We all know what will happen. One state government after another, Labor state governments will fold, and the timber industry will pay the price. The worst thing is it's not only the timber industries which will pay the price. Where will we get our timber from? We'll have to import it. Will it be sustainably harvested overseas? This is the question that we want answered by the minister today. Let's hear him stand up today and say: 'All the timber that we begin importing as a result of my policies will be sustainably harvested. There'll be no issues, and it will all be done in the same way that we harvest timber here.' Let's hear him stand up and say that. It'll be a bit like his commitment that all batteries installed would be done safely and to all technical specifications. Did we get that guarantee? No, of course not. Will

speaker: Dan Tehan
heading: REGULATIONS AND DETERMINATIONS · Carbon Credits (Carbon Farming Initiative-Improved Forest Management in Multiple-use Public Native Forests) Methodology Determination 2026; Disallowance
text: we get a guarantee on this? No, we will not. Despite the fact that we are having this debate publicly in the parliament, understanding how this net zero regulation has come about has been cloaked in mystery. Work by the government to activate this net zero regulation began in 2024 by the Australian National University. Despite multiple FOI requests—why doesn't this surprise you? Remember, the sun was going to shine in, the Australian sun was going to shine in. Despite multiple FOI requests, which have been blocked, the modelling on which this regulation rests has never been released publicly. They believe in their cause so much, but of course they cannot release— Yes, that's it! The consultation period for the enactment of this regulation ran over summer for just 28 days. There is no transparency. There's as much transparency on this as there is in the Capacity Investment Scheme. Of course, there is so much so much transparency around that one—billions and billions of dollars being locked away, and we

speaker: Dan Tehan
heading: REGULATIONS AND DETERMINATIONS · Carbon Credits (Carbon Farming Initiative-Improved Forest Management in Multiple-use Public Native Forests) Methodology Determination 2026; Disallowance
text: get nothing from the government. There is no transparency. I'm going to allow others to speak, because we've only got 40 minutes. I would like to go my full time, but I want to make sure there are others in the debate. These transparency issues are our substantial concern. First of all, it's net zero window dressing. Second, carbon leakage will increase. Third, and most importantly, is where those opposite should apologise today in this place. I don't think the minister has the word 'apology' in his vocabulary, but this is where he should apologise. This will cost forestry jobs. Not only that—it will hurt prime agriculture land. NSW Farmers has raised that concerns the park declaration restricts private native forestry on adjacent private holdings and creates pest, weed and fire management risks. I saw the minister scoffing about this. It is creating a bad precedent, and that is why this House must oppose Labor's net zero zealotry.

speaker: Darren Chester
heading: REGULATIONS AND DETERMINATIONS · Carbon Credits (Carbon Farming Initiative-Improved Forest Management in Multiple-use Public Native Forests) Methodology Determination 2026; Disallowance
text: timber. In Victoria, look no further than the beautiful St Kilda Pier in Port Phillip Bay. Go to the Parks Victoria website. On the Parks Victoria website, they actually gush about the beautiful aesthetics of the hardwood timber decking as it curves around the bay, giving wonderful viewing opportunities for the people of Melbourne. Every piece of timber used on the decking on the St Kilda Pier is Darwin stringybark, brought to Victoria for a couple thousand kilometres of transport costs and the greenhouse emissions that go with that. That is the hypocrisy of Victorian Labor government. There's not just one example. You can go for a little drive across the western suburbs to the West Gate Tunnel and out onto the Werribee Plain. There's a new structure on the freeway as you drive through the West Gate Tunnel and out the other side. I don't know when we got to a point where you need to have architectural works on the side of a freeway; I think they should

speaker: Darren Chester
heading: REGULATIONS AND DETERMINATIONS · Carbon Credits (Carbon Farming Initiative-Improved Forest Management in Multiple-use Public Native Forests) Methodology Determination 2026; Disallowance
text: of the solution to reducing emissions, because a young re-growing forest absorbs more carbon than a mature deteriorating forest. That's a simple fact. The member for Fremantle says, 'No, it's not.' I invite him to stand up at some point—I'm sure he'll get his opportunity—and he can run through how he came up with this strategy. He was the architect of methodology that Labor's applying here. The assistant minister, Mr Wilson, was the architect of this methodology. Shutting down the Australian native hardwood timber industry is the deliberate design strategy of what he's trying to achieve here. He has stated on many occasions that he hates the native hardwood timber industry. From the wooded suburb of Fremantle, from the heavily timbered suburb of Fremantle, the member for Fremantle has always wanted to shut down the native hardwood timber industry. He was happy when they shut down the industry in Western Australia. He was happy when they shut it down in Victoria. He would love to see all harvesting in the native timber industry end. Tell me that's not true. The silence says it all. This bloke wants to shut down the native hardwood timber industry right across Australia—

speaker: Chris Eyles Bowen
heading: REGULATIONS AND DETERMINATIONS · Carbon Credits (Carbon Farming Initiative-Improved Forest Management in Multiple-use Public Native Forests) Methodology Determination 2026; Disallowance
text: Today, both houses of parliament have an opportunity to back practical climate action. Today, both houses of parliament have an opportunity to strengthen the protection of native forests and koalas. Today, both houses of parliament have an opportunity to back economic activity in regional Australia. It's time for people in both houses to back practical action which backs the regions and to vote down the coalition's move to disallow the native forest management method. Voting this down will be a win for New South Wales communities in particular, because the establishment of the Great Koala National Park is expected to generate, with this scheme, $200 million in regional economic activity. We think that's a good thing. It's also going to protect 12,000 koalas, 36,000 gliders and the habitat of more than a hundred threatened species. We think that's a good thing. It's pretty hard for the member for Wannon to surprise me these days, because I thought I'd heard it all. I know that he's an extremist. I know that

speaker: Chris Eyles Bowen
heading: REGULATIONS AND DETERMINATIONS · Carbon Credits (Carbon Farming Initiative-Improved Forest Management in Multiple-use Public Native Forests) Methodology Determination 2026; Disallowance
text: the member for Wannon is run by the IPA and ADVANCE and he's after the 'Sky after dark' vote and he's taking the Liberal Party further right on climate than it's ever been before, which is a big call—hard to do. But I've got to admit I was surprised—gobsmacked, in fact—to hear the member for Wannon say, 'National parks—what do they deliver? Noxious weeds and feral animals.' National parks are a great Australian institution that have had bipartisan support, to be fair. Governments of both persuasions, and federal and state, have built a great estate of national parks through our country that we can be proud of, that people from around the world come to visit and that families visit on a daily basis. They protect our beautiful natural and vital resources. And what does the member for Wannon say about national parks in Australia? 'Noxious weeds and feral animals—terrible things, our national parks.' I've heard it all now. You can only go so far right. I know that you

speaker: Chris Eyles Bowen
heading: REGULATIONS AND DETERMINATIONS · Carbon Credits (Carbon Farming Initiative-Improved Forest Management in Multiple-use Public Native Forests) Methodology Determination 2026; Disallowance
text: take your marching orders from the Institute of Public Affairs and ADVANCE and you're after that 'Sky after dark' vote. You're fighting with One Nation over that. But, really, we've heard it all now. The improved native forest management method is a simple premise. It gives states a way to earn income from carbon credits, if they reduce logging, that they can then invest in those communities and help the workers. It's a voluntary method. States aren't obliged to use it. Some states will; some states won't. New South Wales clearly will. The voluntary method gives states sensible options and gives communities access to economic diversity. A state government can elect to reduce its logging in certain forests in exchange for earning carbon credits, ensuring fewer trees are cut down, there's greater habitat protection for Australian wildlife, and local economies remain supported. This method was initiated by the New South Wales government. The member for Wannon thought that was a revelation. It's all on the public record. It's part of

speaker: Chris Eyles Bowen
heading: REGULATIONS AND DETERMINATIONS · Carbon Credits (Carbon Farming Initiative-Improved Forest Management in Multiple-use Public Native Forests) Methodology Determination 2026; Disallowance
text: the process. The New South Wales government did instigate this. It was independently assessed by the Emissions Reduction Assurance Committee as meeting the legislated offset integrity standards. It'll deliver emissions reductions and improve environmental conditions and biodiversity by protecting native forests. The other person involved in the establishment of this method is Professor Andrew Macintosh. I don't always agree with Professor Macintosh. He is a critic, by and large, of the offsets regime. Here we have a person who has criticised the offsets regime more broadly, but he has specifically designed this one because he believes it has high integrity. He believes it is one which can actively support biodiversity and emissions reduction. So, if even someone who is deeply sceptical of the offsets regime thinks this is a good method, maybe it's an opportunity for members in both houses to reflect on that. I do want to thank the leader of the Greens for her engagement on this issue and the majority of the Greens party room who will

speaker: Chris Eyles Bowen
heading: REGULATIONS AND DETERMINATIONS · Carbon Credits (Carbon Farming Initiative-Improved Forest Management in Multiple-use Public Native Forests) Methodology Determination 2026; Disallowance
text: be supporting this side of the House and opposing the disallowance motion. I simply say this to every member of the House: if you're a Green or not a Green, if you believe in climate action—if you're voting on a bill or a motion in relation to climate change and you're in the Liberal Party, the National Party or One Nation, you're probably on the wrong side. I know some Greens senators have taken a different view and have chosen to vote with the Liberals and Nationals and One Nation. I simply say this: you tried that before on the CPRS, and you set back climate action in this country by decades. That is something that the Greens party should always be ashamed of. This is practical action, and the majority of the Greens have taken a more practical and sensible course today. On these sensible measures, the member for Fremantle and I have agreed to make some small adjustments to the process which will enable the Clean Energy Regulator

speaker: Chris Eyles Bowen
heading: REGULATIONS AND DETERMINATIONS · Carbon Credits (Carbon Farming Initiative-Improved Forest Management in Multiple-use Public Native Forests) Methodology Determination 2026; Disallowance
text: to give effect to the New South Wales government's commitment to limit the sale of ACCUs generated within the Great Koala National Park to a specified class of entities. It'll apply only to projects under this method and only where a state government chooses to opt in to those requirements. In addition, my honourable friend has written to the Emissions Reduction Assurance Committee seeking advice on variations to the method, including the amount of forest that must be protected against established harvesting baselines before projects can receive any carbon credits—rising to 30 per cent for projects registered from 1 July 2030—and clarifying the definitions of plantation forests and native forests. The ACCU scheme is an important part of Australia's pathway to net zero. I know I run the risk of triggering members opposite by mentioning net zero, but it is an important part of it.

speaker: Chris Eyles Bowen
heading: REGULATIONS AND DETERMINATIONS · Carbon Credits (Carbon Farming Initiative-Improved Forest Management in Multiple-use Public Native Forests) Methodology Determination 2026; Disallowance
text: I just talked about the economic development opportunities, investment and jobs created in regional Australia. The ACCU methods can not only help drive emissions reduction; they can also create economic growth and opportunities for landholders, regional communities and businesses. The honourable member for Gippsland said we need to go out to regional Australia. Well, I have walked Arnhem Land, and I have inspected the savanna burning method, for example, with the First Nations groups implementing that method. I have seen firsthand the economic opportunities, the growth and the jobs created for our First Nations people in Arnhem Land. A couple of weeks ago I was in Yass looking at the soil sequestration methods and the wealth created and the improvements in soil for farmers and the improvements in productivity created by these methods. So I say to the National Party and the Liberal Party that they should get out more and they should talk to those farmers who want to take these methods up. They should talk to those groups

speaker: Chris Eyles Bowen
heading: REGULATIONS AND DETERMINATIONS · Carbon Credits (Carbon Farming Initiative-Improved Forest Management in Multiple-use Public Native Forests) Methodology Determination 2026; Disallowance
text: who want to participate in these methods. We did implement the Chubb review on coming to office, which has seen enhanced integrity and expanded opportunities for regional Australia. The Climate Change Authority's latest review of the scheme, released just last week, found it robust and that it remains fundamentally sound and important to Australia's climate policy framework. So we'll continue to take sensible and practical steps, and I thank those honourable members in this House and in the Senate who are supporting it. There once was a time when those on the conservative side of politics saw the value in conserving the environment. I've often thought that you're not really a conservative unless you care about conserving the environment. I do want to pay tribute, however, to Senator Andrew McLachlan, who has indicated he will be voting with the government—a Liberal senator who'll be voting with the government. He has shown courage and a practical approach, and he's to be congratulated for that. It's also the case that the Liberal

speaker: Chris Eyles Bowen
heading: REGULATIONS AND DETERMINATIONS · Carbon Credits (Carbon Farming Initiative-Improved Forest Management in Multiple-use Public Native Forests) Methodology Determination 2026; Disallowance
text: Party wants you to support markets. This is a carbon market. This is a market mechanism. We on this side of the House support the operation of the market. Those opposite oppose it. We want to see regional communities benefit from sensible climate policies. We're focused on practical outcomes. We're focused on emissions reductions and jobs creation at the same time. I also want to thank the honourable member for Fremantle, my assistant minister, who's done such good work on this. He's to be congratulated for this outcome, as well. I thank those members and senators who today will be voting for practical environmental protection and for economic growth and who will be voting against ideologues on the other side who don't believe in emissions reduction and want to see regional communities suffer.

speaker: Alison Penfold
heading: REGULATIONS AND DETERMINATIONS · Carbon Credits (Carbon Farming Initiative-Improved Forest Management in Multiple-use Public Native Forests) Methodology Determination 2026; Disallowance
text: We just heard a speech from the Minister for Climate Change and Energy that did not mention jobs and did not mention real people once. Well, Minister, my electorate has the Herons Creek mill. The Green Mill is now shut. Jobs are lost. Jobs started to be lost on Father's Day, when the New South Wales government announced the moratorium. Can you imagine the impact? It's fine for you here in Canberra to say 'economic development'. There's no economic development in Herons Creek. I'll tell you what there is; there's job losses. There are job losses, and not just for the mill at Herons Creek. The impact is on mills up and down the coast. Another one of my timber mills has seen the availability of logs smashed, and the demand for their timber is being cut by a third. That's a small business operating in a small community. These are the impacts that are already being felt in the community. I've also got the Australasian Sports Floors manufacturer. They

speaker: Josh Wilson
heading: REGULATIONS AND DETERMINATIONS · Carbon Credits (Carbon Farming Initiative-Improved Forest Management in Multiple-use Public Native Forests) Methodology Determination 2026; Disallowance
text: As the minister explained, the government are going to oppose this motion because we support the sensible further development of Australia's land-based emission reduction efforts through what has become the largest, highest quality and highest integrity carbon market in the world. We support the bringing forward of carefully designed and rigorously developed methods that expand opportunities for emission abatement while delivering new economic opportunities that are overwhelmingly located in rural and regional parts of Australia and significant improvements in environmental conditions and biodiversity. And we support outcomes that protect our native forest estate and therefore protect our precious distinctive Australian biodiversity. And that's precisely what the integrated native forest management, or INFM, method can deliver. The project put forward by the New South Wales government under the INFM method is part of their commitment, as the debate has considered, to establish the Great Koala National Park. It will support the protection of 176,000 hectares of native forest on which koalas depend—forest that is home to a hundred at-risk native species—while

speaker: Josh Wilson
heading: REGULATIONS AND DETERMINATIONS · Carbon Credits (Carbon Farming Initiative-Improved Forest Management in Multiple-use Public Native Forests) Methodology Determination 2026; Disallowance
text: creating significant new economic opportunities that we on this side of the House support. And that's why the INFM method is supported by the Nature Conservation Council of NSW, the National Parks Association of NSW, the Australian Climate and Biodiversity Foundation and Greenpeace, among others. It is disappointing that the Nationals bring this motion, particularly when their apparent remit is the interests and wellbeing of people in rural and regional Australia. It is disappointing that they would seek, through this motion, to undermine the carbon farming system that has emerged to such varied and positive effect over the last 15 years in the communities that they represent. I say that knowing that the ACCU scheme is appreciated in rural and regional communities, where the enormous value of having options to diversify economic activity while caring for country is seen very clearly. I say that while we work with Meat & Livestock Australia on an updated livestock method. I say that while we work to deliver an updated reforestation and forestation

speaker: Josh Wilson
heading: REGULATIONS AND DETERMINATIONS · Carbon Credits (Carbon Farming Initiative-Improved Forest Management in Multiple-use Public Native Forests) Methodology Determination 2026; Disallowance
text: method, where stakeholders from around the country—but particularly landowners, farmers and people in rural and regional Australia—come to us, come to the government and say how grateful they are that this vital opportunity in Australia is being maintained and indeed expanded. I say that, as the minister has noted, knowing the incredible extent to which the savannah fire management method has protected 34 million hectares in northern Australia, delivering $59 million a year to project operators, 75 per cent of which are First Nations led businesses. The INFM method recognises the carbon sequestration value that's achieved when there's a commitment to a substantial cessation of logging in state managed native forests, while rigorously calculating and applying conservative discounts for the possibility of carbon leakage. We are very conscious on this side of the House, through this new method and through the ACCU scheme as a whole, of just how critical it is to deliver substantial emissions abatement in a variety of ways, in every area of Australia's landscape and its

speaker: Josh Wilson
heading: REGULATIONS AND DETERMINATIONS · Carbon Credits (Carbon Farming Initiative-Improved Forest Management in Multiple-use Public Native Forests) Methodology Determination 2026; Disallowance
text: economy in a way that's predictable, forward-looking and fair. We make no bones on this side of the House about the fact that the ACCU scheme is helping to combat dangerous climate change, whose effects will be felt most sharply on the social and economic circumstances of people in regional, rural and remote Australia. The obligation and the responsibility on all of us to take that seriously is something that this side of the House understands, while those on the opposite side of the House completely ignored it and put their heads in the sand about it for the 10 years while they were at the helm of the ship. We know that helping to combat dangerous climate change by emissions avoidance and sequestration, and the support that the ACCU scheme provides, is critical. It's absolutely essential to a sensibly managed process of decarbonisation—one in which Australia continues to reduce our national emissions profile, in keeping with our ambitious 2030 and 2035 Paris climate agreements, but does so without jeopardising

speaker: Josh Wilson
heading: REGULATIONS AND DETERMINATIONS · Carbon Credits (Carbon Farming Initiative-Improved Forest Management in Multiple-use Public Native Forests) Methodology Determination 2026; Disallowance
text: the viability of emissions-intensive and trade exposed industries. The INFM method, a new ACCU method, will make a small but substantial new contribution to that task while supporting a new much needed native forest sanctuary for at-risk Australian flora and fauna, not least of which is the koala. As I have to keep pointing out, the feature of the ACCU scheme that appears to have been deliberately ignored by those opposite—in bringing this motion and in general—is the extent to which the carbon market is creating opportunities for communities in regional and rural Australia. Economic diversification, economic viability, investment in a whole variety of ways, whether it's in the clean energy transition or in carbon farming—that is supporting the vitality of regional and rural communities. That's something that we see clearly, and that's something that we will continue to support. This motion seeks to block the protection of Australian native forests. It seeks to block, for no good reason, a new piece in a vital patchwork quilt of land based

speaker: Josh Wilson
heading: REGULATIONS AND DETERMINATIONS · Carbon Credits (Carbon Farming Initiative-Improved Forest Management in Multiple-use Public Native Forests) Methodology Determination 2026; Disallowance
text: greenhouse gas abatement, at a time when we need to keep doing as much of everything, everywhere, all at once as we can possibly manage: renewable energy and storage, electrification of transport and decarbonisation of industry, agriculture and our built environment. Land based abatement, and all the many good things that brings with it for environmental repair and restoration, particularly for rural and regional communities, is a critical part of that. I'll tell you that the people that come to see the minister and me express that in no uncertain terms, all of the time. The ACCU scheme methods—

speaker: Josh Wilson
heading: REGULATIONS AND DETERMINATIONS · Carbon Credits (Carbon Farming Initiative-Improved Forest Management in Multiple-use Public Native Forests) Methodology Determination 2026; Disallowance
text: including this new method, are a critical element of that process, delivering abatement and sequestration that will help protect this country from dangerous climate change, which is the greatest risk that faces the communities that you purport to represent. speaker: Helen Haines
heading: ADJOURNMENT · Cheaper Home Batteries Program
text: I rise today to speak on the Cheaper Home Batteries Program. I'm proud that a policy I first brought to this parliament in 2022 is now helping half a million Australian households and small businesses by cutting energy bills and putting more money back into people's budgets. Australian households and small businesses deserve reliable and affordable essential services like energy. People are feeling the pressure of high living costs, and power bills are a big part of this. Rooftop solar has helped thousands power their appliances at next to no cost when the sun is shining. But people who invested in rooftop solar years ago are getting less return from solar feed-in tariffs than they used to. Home batteries store that energy for when it's needed. The people of Indi sent me to parliament to get practical things done, and it was with their mandate that I pushed to include household batteries in the Small-scale Renewable Energy Scheme. I introduced my Cheaper Home Batteries Bill in 2022 and again in

speaker: Helen Haines
heading: ADJOURNMENT · Cheaper Home Batteries Program
text: 2023. I also met with the Minister for Climate Change and Energy multiple times to discuss the proposal, and I thank him for his constructive engagement over a long period of time. In 2025 the government adopted this policy—even keeping the name—and I congratulate them for doing so, because good ideas are always worth backing wherever they come from. I am now deeply concerned, though, by reports of battery cowboys rorting the system by abusing unlicensed contractors and falsely claiming batteries have been installed when they have not. Last year I spoke with the Minister for Climate Change and Energy about door-to-door salespeople seeking to exploit the scheme. Rorting taxpayer money is a scourge, and any dodgy doorknockers and battery cowboys must absolutely be stamped out. The minister has said that 315 complaints have been made about the SRES; that's a very small proportion in the context of thousands of legitimate batteries successfully installed and reducing household energy costs. Indi has installed 4,108 cheaper home batteries with more than 100,000

speaker: Helen Haines
heading: ADJOURNMENT · Cheaper Home Batteries Program
text: kilowatt hours of capacity; that's the third-highest take-up of cheaper home batteries in Victoria. Wodonga, Baranduda and surrounding communities have led the way, installing more than 900 batteries. Wangaratta and the King Valley together have installed more than 550, followed by 240 in Benalla, 180 in Beechworth and about 130 each in Mansfield, Euroa and surrounds. As I often say in this place, many regional Australians are embracing the energy transition and helping to drive it. Every one of these batteries in Indi is a household or business sharing in the benefits of the transition, with lower power bills and more reliable and more secure power when they need it most. Peter, from Bright, is a great example. His property is supplied by a single power line. When a tree falls or a storm damages that line, he and his neighbours lose their power. His water pump also stops, leaving him and his wife without running water. Since installing a home battery, Peter can keep his fridge and water pump

speaker: Helen Haines
heading: ADJOURNMENT · Cheaper Home Batteries Program
text: running when there's a blackout, and his quarterly energy bill has dropped from $1,100 to about $140 a quarter. That is a huge saving for a retiree on a fixed income. Peter's story is just one of thousands across Indi where home batteries are making a real difference. Strong uptake shows that cheaper home batteries are a resounding success—but too many people still miss out. The next step is that the government must help renters and low-income households to access solar and battery options, so that they too can reduce their power bills and increase their energy security. Portable, low-power 'plug and play' battery and solar systems are increasingly common in Europe and the United States, and we should look at how these options could work safely here in Australia. As the policy marks its first year, I congratulate the Prime Minister, the Minister for Climate Change and Energy and the people of my electorate of Indi, who championed cheaper home batteries. This program is a powerful example of the local impact and national influence in working together, as an Independent member of parliament with the people of Indi and with the government of the day, to achieve something that benefits the whole nation.

speaker: Sam Birrell
heading: CONSTITUENCY STATEMENTS · Central North Renewable Energy Zone
text: I rise to talk about a tiny bit of commonsense which has found its way into a state somewhat devoid of commonsense because of the governance of the Victorian Labor government. But thankfully a logical decision has been forced on a bad government by a community that did not back down. The Central North Renewable Energy Zone has been scrapped because of the efforts of the community, the farmers and the people in the wider area. What was the Central North Renewable Energy Zone? Well, someone decided that it would be a great idea to put a renewable energy zone, which was primarily going to be solar projects, in one of the most productive farm areas in Victoria. Part of it was the East Shepparton irrigation system, which grows all sorts of things including dairy pastures and fruit, and part of it was the Dookie plains cropping area, cropping land that is so good that the yields of wheat, barley and canola are significantly higher than the nation's average. The

speaker: Sam Birrell
heading: CONSTITUENCY STATEMENTS · Central North Renewable Energy Zone
text: community said, quite rightly, 'This is farming land. Why do we want to put solar projects all over it?' The government said, 'No, no, you're going to have a renewable energy zone, and it'll be great.' And the community said 'It won't be great.' They fought against it. They produced report after report. They were put through stress and concern, which they should never have been put through, but they fought back. The efforts of Protect Dookie and the Goulburn Valley, led by Jodie Fleming, Hannah Harmer and many farmers across the region including Chris Ludeman, have led the government to finally come up with a little bit of commonsense and scrap this renewable energy zone. As I've said in this place before, renewable energy has a place, but it's not on agricultural farmland that is there and, for many, many generations, has provided incredible yields of winter and summer crops. Renewable energy needs to have social licence. It also has been shown overseas and in a lot of modelling

speaker: Sam Birrell
heading: CONSTITUENCY STATEMENTS · Central North Renewable Energy Zone
text: that renewable energy is useful in a grid only up to a certain percentage. The madness of governments that think that Australia can run heavy industry and an industrial economy on 80 plus per cent renewable, therefore intermittent, energy is a fallacy. Let's get this energy transition right by respecting communities, respecting agricultural land and understanding both the benefits and the limitations of renewable energy. Well done to the people of Dookie and the Central North Renewable Energy Zone. Thank goodness it's gone.

speaker: Elizabeth Watson-Brown
heading: BILLS · Passenger Movement Charge Amendment Bill 2026; Second Reading
text: just want to be clear: we can't support reforms that will make the cost of living worse for people. In an affordability crisis, the Greens won't apologise for opposing a Labor government move that will make things even harder in these difficult times for everyday people. Just quickly on climate, this bill is not going to have any impact on reducing emissions from air travel. There's no other way to get overseas; people will still fly. The extra fee is not going to deter them; it will just make things harder for them. If the government were serious about reducing emissions from air travel, they'd fast-track high-speed rail—it'd be great for all of us—so we can start to make significant reductions in domestic flights. Labor would rather tax your trip to Bali than tax a gas corporation. Get this—gas corporation Santos made $47 billion over the last 10 years and paid no tax. But Labor are not willing to tax them. They are, however, happy to tax your next holiday.

speaker: Elizabeth Watson-Brown
heading: BILLS · Passenger Movement Charge Amendment Bill 2026; Second Reading
text: Hidden in the last federal budget, the government quietly announced a $10 hike in airline ticket charges—paid by the customer, not the airline. Yes, you heard me right: the government wants to increase airline ticket charges—not abolish hidden fees, but increase them. No-one likes those charges. You go online to see how much a flight costs, plan your itinerary and then discover the hidden fees. For some flights, these fees can be hundreds of dollars per person, making an annual holiday simply unaffordable for many families. It's not as if the government has no other choice. If it needs more money for services, it could do what nearly 70 per cent of Australians actually want and tax gas exports. The government already collects the same amount of money from passport fees that it gets from the gas industry. It collects five times the amount from visa applications that it gets from the gas industry—what a joke! But it's not funny. My message to Labor is this—don't tax the family holiday; tax gas.

speaker: Elizabeth Watson-Brown
heading: ADJOURNMENT · Climate Change
text: 'Now is not the time to talk about climate change.' That's what the Prime Minister said in response to the climate fuelled tragedy in Nepal. These events are a climate warning. Climate change is exacting a terrible, tragic price. The people of Nepal are responsible for a vanishingly small amount of the emissions that have caused this tragedy, yet they are the ones who are paying the heart-wrenching, devastating cost. While the Prime Minister was in the Pacific recently, talking up Australia's climate credentials, the Minister for Resources was cutting the ribbon on the Beetaloo basin gas fracking project—yet another Labor approved climate bomb. Just days later, the Labor government waved through yet another coalmining expansion in Queensland, the 37th new fossil fuel project approved by Labor. So when is it okay to talk about climate change? Is it when the next glacier melts and sweeps away an entire town? Is it when Brisbane experiences another one-in-a-100-year flood? Is it when bushfires set New South Wales on fire again? This

speaker: Elizabeth Watson-Brown
heading: ADJOURNMENT · Climate Change
text: is what 30 years of kicking the can down the road looks like. Labor knows exactly what the opening of new coal and gas projects is doing to our climate and environment, but they approve them anyway. They are approvals of fossil fuel projects that directly contribute to disasters; they have contributed to the deaths of thousands of innocent people in just the last few weeks. The United Nations warned last week that the coming El Nino is expected to be the strongest since records began. We are six days out of winter and, in Queensland, there are fires burning in the Lockyer Valley. We wake up to bushfire warnings on the morning radio. A new report from the Climate Council revealed that a conservative estimate of sea-level rise puts 250,000 Australian homes at risk by 2100. That's over $850 billion in damages by the end of the century. This is the price of approving new coal and gas mines, and that price isn't paid by politicians. It's paid by

speaker: Elizabeth Watson-Brown
heading: ADJOURNMENT · Climate Change
text: everyday people. So when is it okay to talk about climate change? Do we have to wait until yet another Australian resources minister retires from politics and goes on to work for a fossil fuel company? The environment, the climate and everyday Australians deserve a government that puts them ahead of the obscene profits of fossil fuel companies, like Santos and Woodside. Can we just tax gas companies already? We know that more than half of the gas Australia exports is given away for free, with zero royalties or PRRT paid by gas companies. We know that a 25 per cent tax on gas exports would raise $17 billion every year. We know that a 25 per cent tax on gas would encourage gas companies to sell to the domestic market first and at a lower cost. A gas export tax solves all of these problems at once. But, instead of imposing a holistic 25 per cent tax on gas companies, the Labor government announced they would require gas companies

speaker: Elizabeth Watson-Brown
heading: ADJOURNMENT · Climate Change
text: to reserve 25 per cent of their supply for the domestic market. But we don't have a gas supply problem; we have a gas export problem. Now they're watering down that already watered down policy. All they're going to require gas companies to do is simply supply up to 25 per cent of their supply for the domestic market. Companies can already supply up to 100 per cent of their gas to the domestic market if they want. But why would they when they're making absolutely obscene profits exporting our gas for free? Can we just tax gas companies already?

speaker: Dan Tehan
heading: BILLS · Clean Energy Finance Corporation Amendment (Protecting Australian Farmland) Bill 2026; Second Reading
text: I move: That this bill be now read a second time. This bill is aimed at stopping Labor's net zero agenda from literally destroying our way of life. This is about making sure we're protecting our way of life, and we have to protect our way of life, because Labor's net zero obsession is harming and hurting it in so many ways. The latest example is what is happen to our farmland. We are seeing our farmland being harmed. Communities are being harmed because Labor are pursuing the wrong priorities. There was an example in the last term of government in my electorate in and around a town called Simpson. We saw a foreign company, a German reinsurer, come in and purchase dairy farms and beef farms so that they could be planted with trees so that it could get the carbon credits from them. The community was up in arms. No-one consulted with the community about this. No-one said to the community, 'You're going to see massive change in

speaker: Dan Tehan
heading: BILLS · Clean Energy Finance Corporation Amendment (Protecting Australian Farmland) Bill 2026; Second Reading
text: belief that we've got another example down at Rushy Lagoon, in Tasmania, where not only a foreign company came in and bought a prime piece of agriculture land but the government helped facilitate it by getting the Clean Energy Finance Corporation to help fund it. You've got a government organisation, the Clean Energy Finance Corporation, saying, 'Yes, we're happy to tip in $69 million to help this overseas company buy this farmland.' Guess what. The poor old Australian farmer, the poor old Tasmanian farmer, who thinks they wouldn't mind using this land as a dairy farm, as a beef farm or for any other purpose—how can they compete with a government organisation that tips in $69 million? It is an absolute disgrace. This private member's bill is all about saying enough is enough. The Clean Energy Finance Corporation cannot step in and help fund a foreign entity to buy Australian farmland. Enough is enough. Who's in support of this? The only people in support of this are the Albanese Labor

text: government—oh, and probably the Greens as well. They're the only ones in support of this. Does the Tasmanian state government think it's a good idea? No. Does the local farming organisation in Tasmania think this is a good idea? No. Does the local community think this is a good idea? We've got the so-called champion of regional and rural Australia here sitting opposite, the member for Eden-Monaro. Did she intervene to do anything? No. Nothing was done to protect these regional and rural communities. And enough is enough. We've got to put an end to this. The Clean Energy Finance Corporation should have known better. If they were stepping in to fund something like this, they should have known that this wasn't viable. If it had been viable, they wouldn't have needed to step in. They are meant to make sure they get a return

speaker: Dan Tehan
heading: BILLS · Clean Energy Finance Corporation Amendment (Protecting Australian Farmland) Bill 2026; Second Reading
text: on what they're lending, yet they've done some dodgy deal with an overseas company to buy this land and take it out of the hands of Australian farmers. Well, I say enough is enough, and that is why this private member's bill is so important. I hope those opposite have a think about what is going on here. Could you imagine if the Clean Energy Finance Corporation stepped in and said, 'We're going to buy the Marrickville golf club and plan it with trees'? There would be absolute uproar if they stepped in and said, 'We're going to buy the Marrickville golf club and plant it with trees.' Yet you sit there and are more than happy to allow this to happen to our good farmland. I would love to continue on for the rest of my allotted time, but I also want to make sure that our coalition partners, who are also up in arms about this, get a chance to speak, so I'm going to hand over to my good friend to continue for the last remaining bit of this debate.

speaker: Sam Birrell
heading: BILLS · Clean Energy Finance Corporation Amendment (Protecting Australian Farmland) Bill 2026; Second Reading
text: This, the Clean Energy Finance Corporation Amendment (Protecting Australian Farmland) Bill 2026, is a critical private member's bill. Australia is facing a cost-of-living crisis, and the attack on agriculture is part of what is causing that cost-of-living crisis. Families are paying much more at the supermarket, more for electricity and more for everyday essentials. At a time when people are struggling, government policy should be focused on producing food, supporting farmers and strengthening our regional communities, not attacking them and not attacking agriculture itself. The Rushy Lagoon example that the member for Wannon explained is absolutely perverse in its outcome. More than 21,000 hectares of productive agricultural land was purchased by a foreign investment fund to plant out with pine trees—to stop the farming, stop the economic activity of the local community and plant out with pine trees. That is perverse enough, Member for Wannon. Do you know what makes it more perverse? It's that the Australian taxpayer helped finance it. The Australian taxpayer helped finance the destruction of an

speaker: Barnaby Thomas Gerard Joyce
heading: STATEMENTS BY MEMBERS · Energy
text: I want to go through some names of people who are fighting the intermittent power scourge: Sandra Bourke, Anna Young, Andrew Weiderman, Grant Piper, Katy McCallum, Lauren Lawler and Michelle Park—and there are so many more. People against intermittent power unite! We have to stop this scourge—the transmission lines, the solar panels, the wind towers. Just the other day, Mark Grady came forward and found out that it was incomplete; the state government, following their own legislation, did not abide by section 20A of their own act. How do they appropriate money when they're not in abidance with their own act? I don't know. One would suggest that that might be fraud. speaker: Barnaby Thomas Gerard Joyce

speaker: Jodie Belyea
heading: QUESTIONS WITHOUT NOTICE · Energy
text: My question is to the Minister for Climate Change and Energy. How is the Albanese Labor government helping Australian families to embrace technology that saves them money on their power bills, and what are the obstacles?

speaker: Chris Eyles Bowen
heading: QUESTIONS WITHOUT NOTICE · Energy
text: 540,211 Australian households have embraced the technology of cheaper home batteries to reduce their bills—in many cases, to nothing—and to help reduce bills for everyone across our energy grid, and 2,326 of those have been in the electorate of Dunkley, which I know the member for Dunkley is very pleased with and proud of. The primary purpose of this program is to help Australian families reduce their energy bills and also reduce the use of gas, particularly in the energy system at night, which leads to cheaper bills. But it's also appropriate to note that this program has been very good at creating jobs. There has been a doubling of the number of battery installers in Australia since this program came in. It's now 8,846. Many of those jobs have been created in our suburbs and in our regions. Take Western Sydney. There have been 50 new jobs created at Penrith Solar Centre, which is in the electorate of Lindsay. PSC is a battery installer that many of us know

speaker: Chris Eyles Bowen
heading: QUESTIONS WITHOUT NOTICE · Energy
text: very well. Those 50 new jobs include apprenticeships, installers and support works. RKS in Mitchell, where the Prime Minister and I visited the other day, has gone from nine employees to 21 thanks to the cheaper home battery policy. This is very much a Western Sydney story. I told the House last week that the electorate of Mitchell now has one in eight houses with a cheaper home battery, which is a great result, but I've got more good news for the House. I've got good news for the member for Hume, because the electorate of Hume is now the electorate with the third-highest take-up of cheaper home batteries in New South Wales. I know the member for Hume is a proud Western Sydney MP. In fact, of the seven electorates with more than 10 per cent of the households with cheaper home batteries, five of them are in Western Sydney. We've got Hume. We've got Mitchell. We've got Greenway. We've got Macquarie. We've got Chifley. This is a great

speaker: Chris Eyles Bowen
heading: QUESTIONS WITHOUT NOTICE · Energy
text: result for those people in Western Sydney who are trying to reduce their bills with the support of the Albanese government and with no support from those opposite, who would abolish this program. The member for Wannon has been very clear that this bill-busting program would go if the member for Hume was the Prime Minister of Australia. To those more than 10 per cent of his electorate who have taken up this policy and those who are planning to do it, he would say: 'No more. It all ends.' This program creates jobs for 137 installers in the electorate of Hume, and, for the more than 10 per cent of voters and households in his electorate who have chosen the cheaper home battery policy, they would end it all. There is a clear choice: the Albanese government, which believes in helping Australian households, supporting Australian households in reducing their bills, or the Taylor opposition, which would stop it all because they don't like Australians reducing their bills through renewable energy.

heading: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS · Sovereign Capability
text: in Townsville and in Mount Isa, this government is about getting back to those basic roots that made our economy strong in the first place. speaker: Mary Aldred
heading: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS · Sovereign Capability
text: This motion discusses the Future Made in Australia plan and the agenda associated with it. While I commend the mover's interest in these areas, I do, however, have a few observations to make about the enlivenment of these goals as we stand with things right now. One of the biggest barriers in the cost of energy. Energy is expensive in Australia, and it is getting more expensive. Its affordability is incredibly important if you want to grow, make and manufacture things in my Gippsland region in a country like Australia. Australia used to lead the OECD in productivity. We now languish in the late teens of the top 20, and you can ask why that is. One of the key reasons is energy affordability. We have surging energy costs, which are significantly hindering Australia's industrial productivity. They are dragging down multifactor productivity right across the broader economy. Manufacturing is energy intensive, collectively consuming over 52 billion kilowatt-hours annually. Escalating electricity and gas bills act as a direct tax on operational

speaker: Mary Aldred
heading: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS · Sovereign Capability
text: efficiency. Instead of allocating capital to automation, research and development or workforce upskilling, Australian businesses right now are forced to divert earned capital and vital resources just to keep their lights on. Let me mention two points about recent data that highlights the significant financial pressure confronting the manufacturing sector. We have skyrocketing gas prices. Industrial users have seen domestic gas prices surge, while Australian manufacturers are paying 48 per cent more for gas than they did prior to global supply shocks. While this government can't control all international events, there is an important chronology of events here to take note of as well. The other point I raise is around operational cutbacks. Research from the Australian Industry Group indicates that 62 per cent of manufacturers are suffering significant negative effects from the energy criss. Crucially, only 15 per cent are in a position right now to pass these costs onto consumers. If they do pass these costs onto consumers, that will have an impact on inflation, on the cost

speaker: Jerome Laxale
heading: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS · Sovereign Capability
text: have what we needed. When prices spike during global conflict, Australian families and businesses feel it directly. When supply chains seize up, it is our manufacturers, our workers and our families who wear the cost of this. We've learnt the hard lesson from that period. Countries are stronger when they can make more of what they need themselves. We have the workers, we have the resources, we have the energy and we have the ideas that the world is looking for. This government has turned all those strengths and all those ideas into jobs and investment. It's building supply chains that can withstand the next shock. We don't need to make everything here to be stronger, but we need to back the capabilities that matter most to our security and to our economy: renewable and reliable energy, critical minerals processing, green metals, defence industries and advanced digital technology. The positive results of this policy extend all over Australia. More than 35,000 jobs are supported today at metals-processing facilities and across

speaker: Jerome Laxale
heading: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS · Sovereign Capability
text: the supply chains connected to them in the Hunter, Gladstone, Mount Isa, Port Pirie, Hobart and Whyalla. At Tomago, the Albanese and Minns Labor governments are working together, investing $2½ billion to secure the future of the aluminium smelter. That investment protects more than 1,000 jobs onsite and another 5,000 across the Hunter. At Whyalla, the government has stepped in to maintain operations and keep sovereign steel-making capability in Australian hands. None of this happens by accident. It happens because this government chooses to back Australian industry rather than dare them to go offshore just like the Liberals and Nationals did with our car-making industry a decade or so ago. At the centre of this choice is the National Reconstruction Fund and $15 billion. To date, it has announced 31 investments totalling nearly $2 billion across resources, biotech, artificial intelligence, food and beverage manufacturing, housing and quantum development. Macquarie Technology Group is one of them. Energy policy sits at the heart of all of this. Wind, solar, storage and gas

speaker: Jerome Laxale
heading: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS · Sovereign Capability
text: are all Australian assets, and they should work for Australians first. We've just announced another policy in this space with the domestic gas reservation. We just need to compare that record to the alternative on offer. Under the coalition, energy was an afterthought. They had 22 policies and didn't land one. Four gigawatts left the electricity system, and only one gigawatt came in. Usually, when energy leaves the system, you need to have a plan to replace it, right, because we're only going to use more and more energy as we electrify. But the coalition had no plan. Twenty-four out of the nation's 28 coal fired power stations announced their closure on their watch, and there was not a single plan to replace that capacity. Now they are promising to scrap Rewiring the Nation and to abolish the National Reconstruction Fund. Their alternative is a fantasy. Nuclear power is the slowest and most expensive form of energy available to us today. If you think the coalition are bad, One Nation

speaker: Kate Chaney
heading: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS · Sovereign Capability
text: I thank the member for Forde for this motion. Last month, I released a report called Clean Power : s ecuring WA' s f uture p rosperity . It was built on a year of work, conversations with more than 50 industry leaders and energy experts, and survey responses from 2,300 Western Australians. WA is at a fork in the road. One path keeps us doing what we've always done—digging and shipping, and propping up fossil fuel dependency for as long as it lasts. The other path decarbonises our economy, diversifies what we export and captures more of that value here at home. Trying to do both comes at a cost. WA has to decide whether its future is as a petro state or an electro state. I think the answer is obvious. WA has the sun, the wind, the land and the minerals to be an electro state powerhouse. Green iron alone could grow from a $4 billion export industry today to as much as a $170 billion industry

speaker: Kate Chaney
heading: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS · Sovereign Capability
text: by 2050, supporting close to 20,000 new jobs. We have active projects across eight clean export industries already. There's urgency here, too. WA's mining, transport and agricultural sectors are between 67 and 98 per cent dependent on imported diesel. When the 2026 Iran war sent oil prices spiking, that dependence stopped being a theoretical risk and became a live one. WA is the only state with rising domestic emissions, with downstream emissions from our fossil fuel exports running at roughly 13 times our domestic footprint. What we do in WA doesn't stay in WA. It shapes global emissions outcomes as much as it shapes our own economy. There was broad agreement from the people I talked to across WA. Business and community are ready to move towards a prosperous future built on sun and wind. They can see the opportunity. What's missing is a strong federal and state government commitment to move at the same pace. The federal government's Future Made in Australia agenda has been a valuable start, but

speaker: Kate Chaney
heading: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS · Sovereign Capability
text: there is much more to do, and it needs to be done much faster. My report identifies eight broad policy priorities. Today I want to touch on just one: de-risking clean industry investment. Existing capital is not getting to the projects and the stages where it's most needed, including first-of-a-kind technologies and development-stage funding. WA's pipeline of clean energy projects is largely at the pilot and proposal stage. Project proponents cite, as their primary barrier to progress, the demand certainty or offtake agreements needed to reach financial close. Without strong financial commitments or forward momentum in the next six to 12 months, WA risks losing these projects entirely to other countries with more favourable conditions. Supply-side funding already exists through a suite of government investment funds like the National Reconstruction Fund, which the member has highlighted; the Clean Energy Finance Corporation; and tailored funds like the Green Iron Investment Fund. These bodies have been critical to Australia's clean energy transition so far, But WA's clean industry proponents consistently report struggling

speaker: Tom Venning
heading: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS · Sovereign Capability
text: hour, the state Labor government and then treasurer Tom Koutsantonis intervened. The deal with POSCO fell over, and GFG Alliance, led by Sanjeev Gupta, ultimately acquired the steelworks. Given where we are today, I think it's entirely reasonable to ask: what would Whyalla look like if POSCO had completed that transaction? GFG Alliance, led by Sanjeev Gupta, buy the steelworks, and we all know what happens next. Years of underinvestment, alleged corruption, financial problems and mounting debt follow. Eventually, in February 2025, the state Labor government pushed special legislation that put the steelworks into administration. Nobody should defend GFG's record. While the steelworks was struggling, the South Australian Labor government was pursuing another vision: hydrogen. In 2022, the Labor government committed $593 million to its Hydrogen Jobs Plan, but there was a problem: the economics didn't stack up, and they never did. Private investments in large-scale green hydrogen projects were being abandoned around the world, but not by the South Australian Labor government who were left carrying the baby. Then

speaker: Tom Venning
heading: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS · Sovereign Capability
text: came the great cover up. In February 2025, the government announced it was putting GFG steelworks into administration and, at the very same time, the government quietly shelved its $600 million hydrogen plan. This is all smoke and mirrors. The Premier's explanation was essentially this question: why build a hydrogen plant if there is nobody to buy the hydrogen? Perhaps it should have been asked before hundreds of millions of dollars of taxpayer money was committed. For years, the government sold a vision of green hydrogen, green steel—a world-leading industrial transformation. But when, the economics caught up, the project was shelved. That is the problem I have with the approach to Whyalla. There is too much focus on crafting the narrative and not enough focus on fixing the fundamentals. Eventually reality catches up with ideology. The Commonwealth and state governments have now committed billions more to support the steelworks, but government support alone cannot make an uncompetitive business competitive. What if last year we had spent $593 million not on

speaker: Tom Venning
heading: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS · Sovereign Capability
text: the Hydrogen Jobs Plan—which didn't deliver one electron, by the way—but on the fundamentals? What if, instead of betting so heavily on a hydrogen future that the private sector wasn't prepared to finance, we'd invested in reliable energy infrastructure? What if we'd put downward pressure on the cost of gas and electricity? Where would Whyalla be today? We will never know, but we do know South Australia has the highest industrial energy cost in the developed world, and energy is one of the biggest costs facing the steelworks. My objective is straightforward. I want Whyalla to make steel for the next 50 years. I want good, well-paid jobs in Whyalla. I want a sovereign steel-making capability in South Australia. I want taxpayer money used to build a sustainable business not continually prop up an unsustainable one. The lesson for the next 10 years is clear: stop chasing the next announcement, stop trying to win the next headline and get the fundamentals right: reliable energy, competitive energy, investment, productivity and a commercially viable steelworks. Eventually reality catches up with ideology, and the people of Whyalla deserve a government that deals with reality.

speaker: Kara Cook
heading: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS · Sovereign Capability
text: Australia has everything we need to make more things here at home. We have the resources. We have the energy. We have the workers, the skills and the ideas. And we have an enormous opportunity to take those Australian strengths and turn them into Australian jobs, Australian investment and Australian industries. That is the ambition behind the Albanese Labor government's Future Made in Australia agenda. My electorate of Bonner has a proud industrial base. At Lytton, we have the Ampol refinery, one of only two remaining refineries in Australia, employing almost a thousand people onsite and playing an incredibly important role in our national fuel security. I've been proud to welcome the Prime Minister; Treasurer, Jim Chalmers; and Minister for Climate Change, Energy, Chris Bowen, to the refinery to meet the workers and talk about the importance of the industry we have today and the opportunities ahead. Ampol is a great example of what A Future Made in Australia is all about. We are backing the industrial capability of Australia

speaker: Andrew Willcox
heading: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS · Sovereign Capability
text: working. Gas is too expensive in this country. We've seen a 40 per cent increase in electricity. That's not sustainable to industry. We need reliable, affordable energy that's available 24/7. The net zero fantasy has to stop. Australia is also not being seen as a stable political country. We've got a prime minister who simply can't be trusted. He promised on 97 occasions that power was going to be $275 cheaper, and that's simply not the case. Then he introduced capital gains tax changes, negative gearing changes and changes to trusts. All those things were never taken to the election, so this prime minister can't be trusted. We're considered a politically unstable country, and that's why our manufacturing and heavy industry is moving offshore. (Time expired)

speaker: Tom Venning
heading: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS · Energy
text: Thank you to the member for Groom for bringing this important motion before the House. It's quite telling that we're here talking about affordability and energy reliability on the same day that more than 600 workers were given their redundancy package at the Whyalla steelworks. Six hundred families and 600 jobs are gone, because energy prices in South Australia are way too high and are not reliable. Before the last election, the Prime Minister told Australians that life would be cheaper under him. Four years on, it's worth testing that promise. Food is up 18 per cent, rent is up 24 per cent and skyrocketing, and electricity is up 40 per cent. Under the last coalition government, power prices rose three-tenths of a per cent year on year. Under this government, that number is 8.8 per cent. That is 29 times the rate. Instead of the promised cut of $275 a year, Australian households have spent an extra $23 billion on energy bills. We were told to trust the modelling.

speaker: Tom Venning
heading: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS · Energy
text: Well, here's a number the modelling never mentioned: more than 244,000 Australians are now on energy hardship programs. Despite our nation's abundant resources, energy poverty in Australia is at its highest levels on record. If that is not a sign something has gone badly wrong with the Albanese Labor government's energy policy, then what is? At question time, we asked the minister about energy policy and we got a programmed response. 'Well, Member for Cooke, did you know there are 2,000 cheaper home batteries in your electorate?' That is the minister's response. Yet, last week, the ABC reported that Labor's Cheaper Home Batteries Program is littered with fraud and misconduct. In four months, 95 tip-offs have landed with the regulator, and the reports are serious—mocked up installs, signatures being forged and unlicensed tradies delivering unsafe or broken systems.
