This is another example of a government program being rorted, and it's taxpayers who are paying for it. Of the roughly 3,500 batteries that have been inspected, 62 per cent were found

speaker: Tom Venning
heading: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS · Energy
text: to be substandard. This program should be paused, audited and referred to the independent inquiry before another dodgy dangerous battery is installed. In South Australia, my state, we have a part-time energy grid dominated by wind and solar. It works well when it's sunny and windy, but it does not work well when it is dark and calm. It is this unreliability and the price spikes that come with it that are crippling industries in the regions. As I said before, today, 600 workers in Whyalla lost their jobs because of this government's energy policy. In June, South Australian wholesale prices went above $20,000 a megawatt-hour. To put that into perspective, it would cost $4.50 to boil a kettle of water. A grid that only works when the weather cooperates is not a grid that industry can plan around. It is no shock that our heavy industries struggle to compete in the global market. Australian taxpayers are paying twofold—firstly, through the higher power bills and, secondly, through ongoing bailouts. That's

speaker: Tom Venning
heading: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS · Energy
text: $240 million for Nyrstar, $3.1 billion for Whyalla, $2.5 billion for Tomago—the list goes on. If we as a nation utilised our resources and focused on lowering energy costs, we would have thriving industries, a diversified economy and a more prosperous nation. Energy-intensive industries are falling like dominoes, and, each time, the taxpayers are asked to catch them. There are two ways forward: bail these industries out forever, or give them the energy they can afford and rely on. We cannot bail our way to a competitive economy. The coalition has a plan. We will scrap net zero and scrap Labor's carbon taxes, including the safeguard mechanism, which is sending industry offshore. We will back any technology that delivers affordable and reliable energy. We will not pick winners and losers; we will let the market do its job and bring prices down.

speaker: Luke Gosling
heading: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS · Energy
text: There is enormous economic potential across the Northern Territory, and, in this place, I've spoken often about Territory gold, the best solar radiation in the world. The Territory is at the forefront of Australia's energy transition. Projects like SunCable and Energy North are tapping into the incredible potential of solar energy to power local industry and to meet the energy needs of our neighbours into the future as well. Big IT players like Amazon, Google and Microsoft are very interested in Territory gold to power their datacentre activities in AI and the cloud. This demand taps into the geographical and institutional stability of Australia and our membership of the Five Eyes security arrangement, along with access to the required telecommunications and other infrastructure. But these investments must benefit the community and deliver for our national interest. The PM's new Australian standards for AI data centres will make it clear: if you want to build here, you have to make our economy and society stronger. The rules are clear. Add to

speaker: Luke Gosling
heading: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS · Energy
text: our energy supply; don't drain it. Strengthen the grid; don't weaken it. Use water responsibly and offset your impact. Hire and train Australians; contribute to our science and research; be part of the community, not a stranger behind a barbed wire fence. These expectations put the needs of the Australian people first—where they should be—ensuring our communities benefit directly through jobs, investment in skills and innovation, while strongly supporting Australia's clean energy transition and safeguarding our long-term water security, something I spoke about in this place just this morning. Our federal government will work with the states and territories and market participants to implement the expectations, particularly through the Energy and Climate Change Ministerial Council. Data centres have enormous potential to expand new renewable investment, but it's important we work together across jurisdictions and with industry to get the investment settings right so that we can continue to keep our systems secure and energy prices low for all consumers. However, as Minister Bowen stated, the Commonwealth will not be standing

speaker: Luke Gosling
heading: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS · Energy
text: by and letting a race to the bottom of states and territories falling over themselves to attract data centres at the cost to household bills. At the national cabinet meeting earlier this month, it was agreed that state—and territory, in our case—owned power can be used if the Commonwealth, by the Australian Energy Regulator, is satisfied it won't push up bills or weaken reliability. If a jurisdiction believes that they have state-owned energy that is cheaper than renewable energy, they'll be able to make that case to the Commonwealth for consideration by the energy regulator on a case-by-case basis. But the regulator will have to be convinced that it would put downward pressure on bills and be cheaper than renewables. That's a very high bar indeed, but we've set it high to ensure that household bills don't go up and it doesn't make it harder for other industries to do business. However, given that high bar has been put into position, the Northern Territory chief minister, when asked just last

speaker: Luke Gosling
heading: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS · Energy
text: week about potential savings on power bills from Beetaloo fracked gas, said, 'I would love to say yes. Unfortunately, that's not going to be the case.' So obviously for the Northern Territory, and I gather for some other jurisdictions as well, there'll be a lot more work to do to make that case. Renewables will be king because renewables are cheaper. Since coming to government, we've acted to help with power bill relief, gas price caps and investing in cheap renewables, all of which those opposite the coalition opposed. After a decade of delay, dysfunction and denial under those opposite, under the coalition, our government is now getting on with the job of rebuilding Australia's energy grid with the lowest-cost form of energy, renewable energy. We're acting to replace ageing, expensive power with cheap, reliable energy which takes advantage of our abundant resources, the sun and the wind, and that is the sensible and commonsense way forward for our nation.

speaker: Simon Kennedy
heading: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS · Energy
text: The economy is getting destroyed by these people. If we can't say that in this chamber, I think there's a real problem in parliament right now because I'm meeting small-business owners in my electorate who are going out of business. FJP Manufacturing's energy prices are up 45 per cent for gas, 41 per cent for electricity. They had seven apprentices. They're down to one. Six apprentices have lost their jobs because energy is destroyed and this economy is destroyed. Pick your adjective, but I think it's not worth mincing words here when these are people's jobs in my electorate. These are people's incomes in my electorate. As Bill Kelty said only yesterday, real wages are going down, and it's an insult to the Australian people. The Prime Minister and the Treasurer are insulting people. Right now, when this government is presiding over the biggest collapse of living standards in our living memory. I think the time for politeness and niceties are over, especially if you put it in the light

speaker: Simon Kennedy
heading: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS · Energy
text: that this government promised $275 off bills four years ago. There are only two explanations for that. Either (1) they had no idea how these energy markets worked and got it completely wrong or (2) they understood and made that false promise anyway. They're the only two possible scenarios for them being so wrong about energy bills coming down by $275. Instead, we hear that they're up an average of $1,400. That's not close; that's not even in the same ballpark. Why is the economy so bad? One of the biggest reasons is that energy is so bad. People remember that promise; they also remember the promise about CGT and negative gearing. The problem, as the Prime Minister said, is that 'you can only tell a lie once because people remember it'. What we've seen is a backflip on CGT, we've seen a backflip on negative gearing, we've seen a backflip on trusts, and we've seen a backflip on energy. Small-business owners in my electorate, all through the manufacturing sites

speaker: Simon Kennedy
heading: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS · Energy
text: in Caringbah, all through Taren Point, understand this only too well. The government can talk all it wants about low-cost energy, but it's not delivering it. We continue to rise through the OECD in our energy costs. We hear from the CEO of BHP that Australia is an outlier, and they're looking at investing elsewhere in the world because our energy prices and gas prices are two to four times higher than in the US. We hear the CEOs of Cadbury and Mars say that Australia is no longer economical to invest in because of our energy prices. We hear about Tomago going bankrupt, Whyalla going bankrupt, Nyrstar going bankrupt, Bell Bay going bankrupt and a smelter in Gladstone going bankrupt. All these energy-rich industries are going bankrupt. The only way we are keeping these industries is because this Labor government bails them out, taking the tax dollars of people at home—hardworking Australians. People are out there losing their mortgages, and we're trying to debate which adjective we use for how bad this economy is. They're losing their mortgages—

speaker: Steve Georganas
heading: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS · Energy
text: We know that families are doing it tough out there. All of us in our electorates here can talk to constituents. That's why this government is doing all that it can to put downward pressure on electricity, on energy prices, on supermarket prices and on a whole range of other things. It's easy to criticise and have no policies in place, but it's harder to actually balance all of this and make sure that we're doing all that we can, as this government is doing. For example, we introduced the Cheaper Home Batteries program, reducing the upfront cost of home batteries by around 30 per cent, helping households dramatically cut their energy bills by 90 per cent. I've met constituents, and I speak to constituents in my electorate who have benefited from this program. Families have told me that their power bills are much lower now, their homes are more energy independent and they have more money left over for groceries, school expenses and household costs. This is real cost-of-living

speaker: Steve Georganas
heading: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS · Energy
text: relief. We've also delivered a $1.7 billion energy-saving package, helping households, small businesses, farmers and local governments reduce their energy use and lower their bills. While those on the other side have spent years debating climate change, one of the reasons we're in this position is that there was no energy policy. I think there were about nine different policies that were changed. Just getting the acceptance that we have to go to renewables has delayed us for many, many years. The whole idea is that we have more players in the market and more renewables in the market, which will bring prices down. We understand that lowering emissions and lowering energy costs can go hand in hand, and we know that energy bills remain, as I said, a challenge for many Australians. That's why we've also established the Consumer Energy Resources Taskforce to help households get the most out of new energy technology, compare plans and switch to cheaper offers, because Australians deserve practical help, not political pointscoring. When

speaker: Steve Georganas
heading: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS · Energy
text: gas prices came under pressure, we took action. We introduced the Domestic Gas Reservation Scheme, requiring exporters to make gas equivalent to 20 per cent of exports available for the Australian market. That means more Australian gas for Australian households and businesses, it means putting downward pressure on domestic gas prices, and it means protecting Australian families and industry from global price shocks and volatility such as we've seen in the last few months with everything that's taking place in the Strait of Hormuz. The difference is simple. While the opposition talks about problems, we on this side, the government, are delivering and producing solutions. We are helping families lower their energy bills, we're helping small businesses manage costs, we are strengthening Australia's energy security and we are ensuring that Australian resources deliver benefits for Australian people. So the difference between this government and those opposite is quite simple. When Australians were worried about rising power bills, we acted. When families needed help with the cost of living, we delivered.

speaker: Steve Georganas
heading: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS · Energy
text: When businesses needed certainty, we put practical measures in place to strengthen energy security and lower costs. We are not asking Australians to wait decades for a solution; we are trying to help them here and now through cheaper home batteries, energy-saving initiatives, support for households and small businesses and reforms to keep more Australian gas in the Australian market. That way, we are putting downward pressure on energy costs while building a stronger and more secure energy future. While the opposition talks about the problem, this government is helping Australians pay the bills, because every policy we deliver is focused on one goal: ensuring Australian families, farmers and small businesses have the support that they need to get ahead with affordable and reliable energy. At the last election, when we looked at the policy of the coalition, all we could see was some pie-in-the-sky nuclear plant to provide energy for Australians. It would have taken years and years—and still would take years and years—to develop, with billions and billions

speaker: Steve Georganas
heading: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS · Energy
text: of dollars of cost. Whoever builds this nuclear plant to provide energy will want to recoup their money, so, for the first 20 years, there's going to be no reduction of energy costs. This is what those opposite proposed at the last federal election. We need solutions, we need them now, and this government is taking all the action that we can take to make sure we bring downward pressure.

speaker: Simon Kennedy
heading: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS · Economy
text: believe that money is better off in the pockets of hardworking Australians and their businesses. No-one knows better how to spend that money than you and the businesses Australians own. Unfortunately, this Labor government believe they are better able to spend that money than hardworking Australians. That is why CGT is going up. That is why negative gearing is now taxed. That is why they went after an increased tax on super funds. That is why tax after tax of this government continues to go up through bracket creep and others. Secondly, the coalition has a plan to create a sovereign wealth fund. We are sick of watching windfall gains that we get under mining, gas and resources being sucked up by this government and then spent on general revenue, be it through the growing Public Service or be it through out-of-control rorting in the NDIS or myriad other government programs. We believe 80 per cent of every extra dollar in windfall gains from gas, coal and minerals should be

speaker: David Moncrieff
heading: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS · Economy
text: is. As much as they pay lip service to lower taxes, they refuse to put their money where their mouth is. When given the chance to support another tax cut this year, they voted against it, this time with One Nation on their side. If those opposite had their way, Australian workers would be paying more tax to satisfy the three right-wing parties' appetite for long lunches, government-owned nuclear plants and the reinstatement of property tax settings that locked a generation of Australians out of the housing market. The coalition say that they're all for lower power prices but still baulk at the rollout of cheap, reliable renewables that shield Australians from global price shocks. Their ever-changing energy policy has been a mix of picking winners through government-owned nuclear power stations, letting the market decide and deciding that letting the market decide didn't produce the outcomes that suit their ideology, so Soviet-style long-term underwriting of ageing generation assets was the go. When none of that works, they change the rules

speaker: David Moncrieff
heading: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS · Economy
text: to hide the power price increases when the facts clash with their ideology, as the Leader of the Opposition did when he was energy minister. Under the coalition's energy plan, not only would Australians face higher energy bills; their taxes and insurance premiums would be higher too. Fortunately for those of us who still believe in markets, the clean energy transition is well underway and delivering real savings for the 4.3 million homes and small businesses benefiting from cheap solar, including the 4,447 households in my southern Sydney electorate of Hughes who have taken up our Cheaper Home Batteries Program. They say that they're all for providing more housing, but what more housing? They hardly built any houses during the near decade that they had in office. We just had the member for Grey in here saying, 'Oh, ministers don't build houses.' Under this government, the minister has been building houses. Our housing policies have been producing way more houses than they ever produced. Why are we surprised, when they

speaker: Tony Pasin
heading: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS · Economy
text: In my electorate, the No. 1 issue of concern for constituents is cost of living, so let's start with the basics. If we're serious about fixing the economy and putting downward pressure on the cost of living, we must get the cost of electricity down. Here is the very first and clear difference between the Labor Party and the coalition. For Labor, energy policy is about ideology, emission targets, transmission lines, secret carbon taxes and billions of dollars in subsidies. The coalition knows that futureproofing electricity is very simple. The question is does it deliver affordable and reliable power to Australian households and businesses? For the people I represent in Barker, electricity isn't an ideological exercise. Electricity is about the price of things. It's about producing the food Australians eat; pumping water and running irrigation; crushing grapes and making wine; milling the timber we use to build our homes; running a shop, a pub or a bakery; and keeping the lights on at a local service station. Under Labor, electricity

speaker: Tony Pasin
heading: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS · Economy
text: bills have increased by about 40 per cent. That matters in Barker. When electricity and gas prices rise, farmers pay more, manufacturers pay more, small businesses pay more, food processors pay more and ultimately South Australian families pay more. Labor talks about making Australia a renewable energy superpower. We want to make Australia a production superpower. We know that means more cheaper energy, and it's not hard to do. We live in an energy rich country. Australia is blessed with vast reserves of coal and uranium. Yet Australia and Australians are being denied the full benefit of these resources. The coalition believes that we should be using Australian energy for Australian homes, farms and businesses instead of exporting it to our competitors. A sensible energy policy must back every technology capable of delivering affordable, reliable power. That means including coal, gas, renewables and indeed nuclear energy as part of a balanced energy mix. We will get more Australian gas into the market. We'll keep reliable generation operating for as long

speaker: Tony Pasin
heading: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS · Economy
text: as we need it. We'll lift the ban on nuclear energy. We'll scrap Labor's secretive carbon taxes, including the Safeguard Mechanism. We'll back coal. We'll back gas. We'll back hydro. We'll back nuclear. We'll back batteries and renewables in the right places. The judge for energy policy is affordability and reliability. Cheaper power means cheaper food, cheaper power means stronger small businesses and cheaper power means Barker can keep doing what it does best, which is producing the food and fibre Australians need. That is one of the ways that we will fix the Australian economy. In Barker, we produce food for the world. We're an agricultural powerhouse. Across food and fibre, we're world-class producers and an integral part of the South Australian and Australian economies. Our farmers are already among the most efficient and innovative producers anywhere in the world. They need and are owed a government that is committed to protecting their right to farm. Here, again, is the fundamental difference between the party I represent and the

speaker: Tony Pasin
heading: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS · Economy
text: once-great Labor Party. Labor's net zero policies are now creating incentives for productive Australian land to be bought for carbon projects. We have already seen where that can lead. In Tasmania, Rushy Lagoon has been sold to a UK investment firm for $142 million. A taxpayer backed Commonwealth body, the Clean Energy Finance Corporation, provided $69 million towards that purchase. About 9,000 hectares are expected to be converted into a plantation. Think about what that means. It means that Australian farmers are now competing with foreign investments that are backed by their own government. This is madness. Labor believes government should spend more. Labor believes government should regulate more. Labor believes we should tax more and subsidise more. The Liberal Party, on the other hand, has a plan to fix the economy and protect our way of life, where we have lower taxes, lower immigration, lower regulation and lower energy costs.

speaker: Julie-Ann Campbell
heading: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS · Economy
text: but five times the opposition voted against lower taxes. If the coalition wanted to deliver lower power prices, why are they so dead set against renewables, which we know are cheaper and cleaner, and instead pursuing an energy future of nuclear, something that we know is devastatingly expensive and takes a very long time to deliver? If the coalition wanted to provide more housing, why did they vote against housing policies that would see 75,000 people—young people—getting into their very first home? And, if the coalition wanted to put Australians first, why will they not tell us what they want to cut? If the experience in Queensland has anything to say on that then we know what the playbook is. The playbook is cutting from domestic violence support and from health. In Queensland, that is what we have seen. You can't look at what the opposition says. You can't trust what the opposition has to say, because, again and again and again, we see them do the opposite. So, rather

speaker: Tom Venning
heading: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS · Economy
text: steelworks in Whyalla, in my own electorate—550 jobs gone today—and the smelter in Port Pirie; they have both needed taxpayers to step in. There are only two ways forward. We can either keep patching the bleed with taxpayer bailouts, or we can fix the root cause by delivering cheap, reliable power so our industries can become competitive again. We cannot have A Future Made in Australia without a competitive playing field. The coalition will scrap net zero and back any technology that delivers affordable and reliable energy for households, small businesses and industries that keep our regions running. We will deliver less migration and more homes by linking migration to the number of homes we actually build. We will axe Labor's toxic taxes and deliver a tax back guarantee. And we will establish a future generations fund to pay down Labor's debt and invest in the roads, ports, energy and water infrastructure this country so desperately needs. The coalition's plan is to put Australians first.

speaker: Dan Tehan
heading: STATEMENTS BY MEMBERS · Manufacturing Industry, Energy
text: Yesterday was a harrowing day for the steelworkers at Whyalla. Over 600 of them were told that their jobs no longer existed, yet that night they had to put up with the Minister for Climate Change and Energy going on 7.30 and absolutely gaslighting Australians. This is what he had to say: 'I never quite bought all the hype on green hydrogen.' But he held it out as the green dream that was going to save their jobs. And what happened? Six hundred people and their families today are facing absolute uncertainty. What do you think the energy minister has done to help try and secure those jobs? Absolutely nothing. You've got the hardworking local member here fighting for them, trying to get them their jobs back, and what the energy minister is doing is completely gaslighting them, coming up with statements like his green energy dream was going to deliver them jobs, when all it did was give them false hope. Shame on you!

speaker: Bob Carl Katter
heading: QUESTIONS WITHOUT NOTICE · Energy
text: Prime Minister, you're aware that American and Western Australian policy says no gas exports until all domestic demands are satisfied. Australian gas exporters told the ACCC this year they have sufficient gas to supply Australia while meeting international contracts. Would you agree that a genuine reserve resource policy should reduce east coast gas prices from around $17 to below $7, comparable with Western Australia and world prices. Will you agree to a true reservation for Australia that mandates every gas exporter to supply Australian households and industry first, saving Mount Isa and other light industrial undertakings?

speaker: Anthony Norman Albanese
heading: QUESTIONS WITHOUT NOTICE · Energy
text: I thank the member for Kennedy for his question. I'll answer it and then get the Minister for Resources to supplement my answer. I've stood with the member for Kennedy in Mount Isa a number of times, backing in industry and support in that vital area of Queensland. The member is certainly right that, when it comes to gas reservation in this country, it needs to be an important part of the policy solution that is required. Our resources have provided us with enormous benefit and income from export, but we also need to make sure that gas is available for domestic manufacturing and, particularly, that we learn the lessons of Western Australia, which has successfully had a gas reservation scheme on the east coast, which is what we have been working on—consulting with industry constructively. I look forward to continuing to consult with the member for Kennedy on these issues. I'd ask the minister to add to my answer.

speaker: Madeleine King
heading: QUESTIONS WITHOUT NOTICE · Energy
text: I thank the member for Kennedy for his question. We do agree, as the Prime Minister has said, that we should have a gas reservation policy that mandates that every gas exporter supplies Australian households and businesses first. That is precisely what this government is doing through the development of the national gas reservation scheme. I'm well aware of the Western Australian gas reservation policy, but I do note how difficult it was to pass at the time in 2008. It was visionary Labor policy, and that vision remains. In 2022, this government inherited a gas policy bin fire. Through the Future Gas Strategy, we have methodically set out how gas will work with our net zero emissions targets that have been legislated. Now, with the introduction of and the exposure draft of the national gas reservation scheme, we are continuing this further. The member for Kennedy will know that the announcement of the gas reservation scheme was of great benefit in his electorate. It provided the commercial confidence required

speaker: Madeleine King
heading: QUESTIONS WITHOUT NOTICE · Energy
text: for the private purchase of Phosphate Hill fertiliser. That would have closed without that scheme's being introduced. Member for Kennedy, for your benefit and for the benefit of others in this House, up until a few months ago, another party here supported a gas reservation scheme. The members for New England and for Farrer would be aware of this. The leader of One Nation, Senator Hanson, very much supported a gas reservation policy. Indeed, in March, she introduced legislation for it in the Senate. In June, though, unfortunately for households around the country and for industry, she backtracked on that and is now not supporting a gas reservation policy. We've been very clear on this policy, which is more than can be said of the One Nation Party.

speaker: Dan Tehan
heading: QUESTIONS WITHOUT NOTICE · Green Hydrogen
text: My question is to the Minister for Climate Change and Energy. Last night, the minister said with a straight face, 'I never quite bought all the hype on green hydrogen'. Does the minister recall who said this on 17 November 2023: Australia's hydrogen industry is projected to generate $50 billion in additional GDP by 2050, creating tens of thousands of jobs in regional Australia as Australia transforms to a renewable energy superpower. Or has he wiped this statement from his mind like his promise to lower power bills by $275?

speaker: Chris Eyles Bowen
heading: QUESTIONS WITHOUT NOTICE · Green Hydrogen
text: I thank the honourable member for the question about green hydrogen and Australia's green hydrogen potential. It is the case that it was a few years ago that it was suggested that green hydrogen could play a role in home heating, in car transport. Electric vehicles just overtook petrol vehicles in Australia. Do you know how many hydrogen cars were sold in Australia last year? One vehicle. So there was a lot of hype about green hydrogen in previous years, and I had the view and have the view that green hydrogen will play a role in industrial decarbonisation. I said that on the 7 . 30 Report last night, and, if the honourable member wanted to quote me in full, he could have. I went on to say that, equally, the reports of the death of green hydrogen are exaggerated. Now, it is the case that a lot of things have been said about Australia's potential for green hydrogen over the years. It is absolutely the case that a

speaker: Chris Eyles Bowen
heading: QUESTIONS WITHOUT NOTICE · Green Hydrogen
text: lot's been said about green hydrogen in Australia. For example, I do recall the quote that the honourable member just mentioned. It's also been said: Exporting green hydrogen as a solid will reduce costs, increase safety and simplify overseas processing which will put Australia at the forefront of an emerging renewable energy market leading to new jobs, new business opportunities and environmental dividends. Well said, Dan! Well said. That is exactly what the shadow minister said about green hydrogen.

speaker: Chris Eyles Bowen
heading: QUESTIONS WITHOUT NOTICE · Green Hydrogen
text: Thank you, Mr Speaker. The member for Wannon said it very well—very eloquently did the shadow minister. But he was part of a team, because what he was also doing was supporting his colleagues. It is the case that he was referring to the announcement that the Morrison government was working to continue with international colleagues to establish Australia as a hydrogen export powerhouse. That was a joint press release between the honourable members, the honourable gentlemen, the member for Hume and the member for Wannon—a joint press release, not even singular.

speaker: Chris Eyles Bowen
heading: QUESTIONS WITHOUT NOTICE · Green Hydrogen
text: Promises have also been made to the people of Whyalla and Port Bonython. For example, it was said: "Hydrogen hubs such as this one will consolidate Australia's resource strengths to unlock clean energy and stimulate a potential surge in industrial activity, with benefits to flow on to the region's local communities," Minister Taylor said.

speaker: Milton Dick
heading: MATTERS OF PUBLIC IMPORTANCE · Energy
text: I have received a letter from the honourable Manager of Opposition Business proposing that a definite matter of public importance be submitted to the House for discussion, namely: The Government's failing energy policies crippling industry and households. I call upon those honourable members who approve of the proposed discussion to rise in their places. More than the number of members required by the standing orders having risen in their places—

speaker: Dan Tehan
heading: MATTERS OF PUBLIC IMPORTANCE · Energy
text: Last night we saw something quite extraordinary. On 7.30 , the Minister for Climate Change and Energy declared: … I never quite bought all the hype on green hydrogen … Yet he put $9 billion into green hydrogen! Now imagine if he had bought the hype. Where would we have ended up? $18 billion? $27 billion? Who knows where the taxpayers' largesse would have stopped? On the back of him not buying into the hype on green hydrogen, he also said this on 13 April 2023: Today's release of the annual State of Hydrogen report reinforces that Australia has the foundations to become a global leader in green hydrogen. On 23 May 2024, he said: Now some people might think, oh, you know, is green hydrogen real, is it going to happen? Well, it's already being manufactured right there in Gladstone … I wonder what the member up the back thinks of that. I'm sure we'll hear from him at some stage. On 18 December 2023 the minister said: And

speaker: Dan Tehan
heading: MATTERS OF PUBLIC IMPORTANCE · Energy
text: if we're going to play our role in decarbonising that is one of the key and essential roles that we can play, developing an Australian green hydrogen industry and exporting it. On 18 January 2024 he said: Firstly, of course, our Government wants Australia to be a hydrogen superpower, a green hydrogen superpower. The list goes on and on and on. If this is what the minister thought not buying in was, what the hell is he doing? What is he thinking—or doesn't he think? This is the worry. It's just all green ideology. It's just pure and utter green ideology. And I say to the minister: have you forgotten your promise to the Australian people for $275 off every power bill? Not only that, have you forgotten your promise to the Australian people that you would support manufacturing jobs? As a matter of fact, the Prime Minister went to Whyalla, and he's quoted as saying he was going to 'secure all those jobs'. That's what the Prime Minister said.

speaker: Dan Tehan
heading: MATTERS OF PUBLIC IMPORTANCE · Energy
text: and say it, yet, once the jobs go, he gets asked a question today in question and he won't even take the question. What a disgrace! What an utter disgrace. He just flicks it. Six hundred jobs—just flicks it. I think this is the worst and greatest insult. We have the Minister for Climate Change and Energy spending $150 million on a pre-COP in Fiji and Tuvalu which is all about his so-called presidency—$150 million and no-one's going. As a matter of fact, what I'm hearing is they're all going to Turkiye, and that's really upsetting the minister for climate change. They're all going to Turkiye and they're not going to his, and that's meant to be really upsetting him. But this is the worst part of it. There is $150 million for that, but what are the workers being offered in Whyalla? So far, there is $10 million after being promised that their jobs were secure forever, that the steelworks was secure forever. The Prime Minister won't even own

speaker: Kate Thwaites
heading: MATTERS OF PUBLIC IMPORTANCE · Energy
text: our commitment to Australian manufacturing. Those opposite, when in government, sat by when then treasurer Joe Hockey goaded car manufacturers to leave the country, with, when they left, devastating outcomes for workers in South Australia and in my home state of Victoria. Those opposite sat on their hands while those manufacturers left this country. They goaded them to leave. It is absolutely galling that at this moment those opposite would seek to create an ideological fight over the future of workers in South Australia, who this government is backing. It is a reality that, after a decade of delay, dysfunction and denial, the Albanese government is getting on with rebuilding Australia's energy grid with the lowest-cost form of energy, renewable energy. We acknowledge the reality that our coal-fired power stations are ageing and they are becoming increasingly unreliable. Again, those opposite ignored this for a decade, and Australian energy users have been paying the price. As a government we are working towards cheaper, cleaner energy in our system—a better deal

speaker: Kate Thwaites
heading: MATTERS OF PUBLIC IMPORTANCE · Energy
text: for households. We're focused on the long-term changes that permanently cut bills, make the system fairer and keep the lights on. And we are headed in the right direction. Last year we saw a record number of renewable projects given the green light and millions of Australians benefiting from a cleaner, more reliable electricity grid that will lower energy bills for good. We are seeing households vote with their feet as they realise the benefits of cheaper, cleaner, renewable energy for them. Australia has the highest uptake of rooftop solar in the world. Since July last year, more than 540,000 Australian households and businesses have installed batteries through the government's Cheaper Home Batteries Program. I get to visit lots of these households and talk to the people who have installed a battery. They're quick to show me their apps and to explain how they've been able to take back control of their energy use and lower their power bills. I've met with Glen and Amanda from Templestowe, in the member

speaker: Kate Thwaites
heading: MATTERS OF PUBLIC IMPORTANCE · Energy
text: for Menzies's electorate, a retired couple who are making significant savings on their electricity bills through their rooftop solar and their battery. I've met with John from Mill Park, in the member for Scullin's electorate. John has an electric vehicle, a home charger and solar panels, and he's in credit on his power bill. He couldn't speak more highly of the difference that rooftop solar and a battery are making to him. I've met with Elizabeth and Eric from Cranbourne, in the member for Holt's electorate, pensioners who are benefiting from greater energy independence and lower bills. Elizabeth and Eric are among more than 2,400 households in Holt that have installed a cheaper home battery. Again, they've told me it's given them greater control over their energy bills and greater confidence that they're doing their bit as part of our bid for a cleaner future. Andrew from Diamond Creek, in the member for McEwen's electorate, is part of a family of four using solar panels and a battery to power

speaker: Kate Thwaites
heading: MATTERS OF PUBLIC IMPORTANCE · Energy
text: their home and their pool, helping them to keep the pool going while also keeping their energy bills down. Australians get this. They get that the transition is on. Those opposite have missed the memo. Last month, electric vehicle sales overtook petrol car sales in Australia for the first time, as more drivers chose lower running costs and greater choice. More than 27,000 battery electric vehicles were sold, a new monthly record. In some ways this seems remarkable because it's not so long since a former prime minister from that side told us all that electric vehicles would 'ruin the weekend'. Well, Australians know better, and, again, they're voting with their feet. They're voting with their economic interests and their interests in the future. They know that household batteries and EVs are helping them take control of their power bills and drive down their energy expenses. Of course, those opposite are the same government that offended our neighbours in the Pacific, that stepped away from the global efforts to deal

speaker: Kate Thwaites
heading: MATTERS OF PUBLIC IMPORTANCE · Energy
text: with climate change and that ignored the fact that the entry price to be a serious part of the Pacific family is being serious about climate. Those opposite cannot be taken seriously when it comes to this debate. We have acted to tackle energy bills and we know there is more to do. We've acted to help with power bill relief, through gas price caps and investing in cheap renewables, all of which the coalition opposed. We are also fixing the retail energy market to make sure that customers are getting better deals from energy retailers when it comes to this essential service. The 2026 default market offer, which is set by the independent Australian Energy Regulator, is delivering reductions in prices for all residential and small business customers. We know we need to keep going, and in fact the Australian Energy Market Commission has warned: Delaying the connection of renewable generation and transmission into the market would put upward pressure on residential electricity costs. Yet this is exactly what

speaker: Kate Thwaites
heading: MATTERS OF PUBLIC IMPORTANCE · Energy
text: those opposite are proposing. The coalition's costly coal scheme keeps ageing, unreliable generators running long past their use-by date. These plants do break down without warning, and every breakdown means a price spike. When coal breaks down, household bills go up. Their scheme pours billions of taxpayer dollars into propping up clapped-out coal instead of building the modern grid Australians deserve—renewables backed by hydrobatteries and fast, flexible gas. They have a plan for more breakdowns, for higher prices and for wasted money, and Australians will pay for it. Australians know they will pay for it because we have the track record of those opposite. During the coalition's decade in government, 24 of the nation's 28 coal-fired power stations announced they were closing, and they did nothing to secure our energy future. Australians cannot afford to keep paying the price of the coalition's climate infighting, their denial of what is actually happening. Let's be clear. Our government is on the track of protecting Australian industry, of backing Australian industry, of backing

speaker: Kate Thwaites
heading: MATTERS OF PUBLIC IMPORTANCE · Energy
text: the transition to cleaner, cheaper renewables. In fact, research by the Clean Energy Council in March 2025 found that household power bills could rise by $449 per year by 2030 if we had greater reliance on gas and coal and if renewables were built more slowly. Household bills could rise by $606 per year by 2030 if this occurred and a major coal-fired power plant failed unexpectedly. The energy experts agree that renewables are the cheapest form of energy and the lowest cost way to replace ageing coal. Treasury's modelling report from September 2025 states: Not pursuing net zero by 2050 risks lower economic growth, reduced investment, missed export and employment opportunities, and higher electricity prices. The recent International Energy Agency report found: Across many wholesale electricity markets, especially in Europe, a higher share of renewables in the power mix has consistently led to lower prices. That is what those of us on this side of the chamber get. That is what governments who understand, who are serious about governing

speaker: Kate Thwaites
heading: MATTERS OF PUBLIC IMPORTANCE · Energy
text: and the future of this country, get. Those opposite come in here to score political points from workers who deserve to be backed, who deserve to have a government that is on their side. Fortunately for those workers in Whyalla, this government is on their side, and we will remain on their side as we continue to support Australians on the transition to cheaper, cleaner energy. We are committed to a clean, sovereign, renewable energy future where households and industries reap the benefits of cheaper, clean, reliable energy.

speaker: Tom Venning
heading: MATTERS OF PUBLIC IMPORTANCE · Energy
text: up until this week, made 75 per cent of Australia's structural steel. It is the only place in the country that makes rail. More than a billion dollars of taxpayer money has gone into the steelworks since it entered administration. Money was not the problem. The problem was the fundamentals and the ideology. Steel is made with energy—so is aluminium, so is cement. Under this government, South Australia has the highest prices of power and gas in the industrial world. When the default market offer came out in May, the Minister for Climate Change and Energy told us that, because of renewables, prices were coming down in every jurisdiction. Well, he told another mistruth. He forgot about South Australia, the renewable capital of the nation and the only jurisdiction to see power prices increase. Just down the road from Whyalla is the Middleback Ranges mine that supplies the steelworks. When the wind drops and the sun goes down, the energy costs too much, so they stopped the crusher. Rostering a

speaker: Tom Venning
heading: MATTERS OF PUBLIC IMPORTANCE · Energy
text: workforce around the weather should not be the reality in Australia. It is not how you run a modern, competitive mine and steelworks. A new furnace will not fix that on its own. An electric arc furnace uses a boatload of electricity and uses a boatload of gas. Unless we get the prices down of both, the next owner will only inherit the same issues. Then there is the carbon tax. The Safeguard Mechanism applies to Whyalla. So, while the government is bailing out the steelworks on the one hand, they are taxing it with the other. Whyalla was promised a green hydrogen revolution. What they were delivered was a hydrogen hoax—$9 billion of taxpayer money invested into a pipe dream across this country. In South Australia, $600 million was poured into a hydrogen plant at Whyalla that was quietly shelved in the shadows of the steelworks administration. It was the great cover up of 25 February. Not one electron was generated, and now we have more than 600 workers

speaker: Tom Venning
heading: MATTERS OF PUBLIC IMPORTANCE · Energy
text: in Whyalla without a job. Why is it that Whyalla and regional communities continue to take hit after hit for this minister's green dreams? Why is it that Whyalla Steelworks and other manufacturers continue to lose their jobs overseas because of this minister's green dreams and net zero ideology. In 2023, Minister Bowen had this to say about green hydrogen: Green hydrogen will play a crucial role in our clean energy transformation and will create jobs and spur investment in regional Australia. In 2024, he said: Hydrogen is central to the Australian government's vision for a Future Made in Australia. He also said that he was disappointed and surprised at the Queensland government's decision to pull hydrogen funding. So clearly he's a big supporter of hydrogen. But then we get to 2026, and what do you think Minister Bowen said? Yesterday, he said—

speaker: Luke Gosling
heading: MATTERS OF PUBLIC IMPORTANCE · Energy
text: I want to acknowledge my good friend the member for Jagajaga and her contribution outlining our solid commitment to Australian workers and, in the case of the topic that's being discussed now at Whyalla, to blue-collar workers. We are absolutely committed, as any reasonable person would know with our track record, to the domestic steel manufacturing industry and to securing the long-term future of those steelworks and the local jobs there. The coalition has no credible plan on supporting Australian manufacturing or Australian workers. I've been around long enough to remember Joe Hockey and the coalition forcing the car manufacturing industry out of this country. Whyalla was well addressed by my colleague, so I'll head north. I've spoken before about Territory Gold, which is the best solar radiation in the world that cuts right through the Northern Territory but also some of our neighbouring states. The Northern Territory is at the forefront of Australia's energy transition as we become a renewable energy superpower. It's through projects like SunCable and Energy

speaker: Luke Gosling
heading: MATTERS OF PUBLIC IMPORTANCE · Energy
text: North that we'll tap the incredible potential of solar energy to power local industry, and we'll also, one day down the track, help our neighbours in ASEAN with their energy needs, with renewable energy. Data centres are very topical. I think they're a good example, when done right. I commend our Prime Minister on the outlines for the guardrails that we're putting in around data centres and AI. But the reality is, when the communities are going to benefit and when power prices are not going to go up, some big IT players are very interested in harnessing Territory Gold, through solar, to run data centres. But these investments, as I said, must benefit the community and deliver for our national interests. Those Australian standards for AI data centres have made it clear that if you want to build here, you have to make our economy and society stronger—and that will happen with abundant renewables. Proponents are going to need to add to our energy supply, not drain it. They're

speaker: Luke Gosling
heading: MATTERS OF PUBLIC IMPORTANCE · Energy
text: going to have to strengthen the grid, not weaken it, and they're going to have to use water responsibly and offset impact. Hiring and training Australians will be essential, and our research and development, our sciences, are going to have to benefit. These expectations are important because they put the needs of Australian people first and are possible when you embrace renewables and Australia's clean energy transition. Our federal government is going to work with the states and territories and market participants to implement the expectations, particularly through the Energy and Climate Change Ministerial Council. We all know that data centres will have enormous potential to expand new renewable investment, and it's vital that we work together across jurisdictions and with industry to get those investment settings right so that we can continue to keep our system secure and energy prices low for all consumers. Minister Bowen has stated the Commonwealth will not be standing by and letting it become a race to the bottom of states and territories falling

speaker: Luke Gosling
heading: MATTERS OF PUBLIC IMPORTANCE · Energy
text: over themselves to attract these data centres at a cost to household bills. At the National Cabinet meeting earlier this month, it was agreed that state and territory owned power can be used if the Commonwealth, via the Australian Energy Regulator, is satisfied it won't push up bills or weaken reliability. If a jurisdiction believes it has state owned energy that is cheaper than renewable energy, it'll be able to make that case to the Commonwealth for consideration by the Australian Energy Regulator on a case-by-case basis. The regulator will have to be convinced, however, that it would put downward pressure on bills and be cheaper than renewables. That's a very high bar that will be set to ensure that household bills don't go up and it doesn't make it harder for other industries to do business. However, the Northern Territory Chief Minister, when asked last week about potential savings on power bills from Beetaloo gas, said: I would love to say yes, unfortunately, that's not going to be the case. Well, there you go. From one jurisdiction— (Time expired)

speaker: Anne Webster
heading: MATTERS OF PUBLIC IMPORTANCE · Energy
text: Last night we saw on Four Corners that the Minister for Climate Change and Energy had the audacity to say, 'I never really bought into all the hype about green hydrogen.' I would suggest to the chamber that he was actually the salesman-in-chief. I would go back to April 2023, where Minister Bowen, the Minister for Climate Change and Energy, said: Today's release of the annual State of Hydrogen report reinforces that Australia has the foundations to become a global leader in green hydrogen. Then, six months later, in January 2024, he said: Firstly, of course, our government wants Australia to be a hydrogen superpower, a green hydrogen superpower. And then a year later, in March 2025, he said: Hydrogen, green hydrogen, is really the only game in town when it comes to ultimately supporting the Australian and international industries as they move in the longer term to get off gas. And Australia is one of the few places in the world which can be home to a serious green

speaker: Anne Webster
heading: MATTERS OF PUBLIC IMPORTANCE · Energy
text: hydrogen industry. And he goes on—there are so many quotes that I could provide to the House. The problem is that we now find we have the smelter in Whyalla closing. That was the big promise—that green hydrogen would be able to run that smelter. All of a sudden, what we have instead are 600 jobs gone. While Labor want to declare that they are the government for workers, I don't think losing 600 jobs is the way to be the government of workers. I don't think making bold promise after bold promise, based on ideology and creative thinking, is helping Australia at all. We are seeing more businesses closing and we are seeing fewer people have confidence in this government, and it's for a very good reason. In my electorate alone, we have the renewable rollout under Labor federally and Labor state, and it is all turning to custard. The reason it's all turning to custard is that they don't bother actually checking in with the communities. There is

speaker: Anne Webster
heading: MATTERS OF PUBLIC IMPORTANCE · Energy
text: no social licence for all of the renewable that is ploughing through prime agricultural land. That's a problem. That's a problem in my electorate. If Australia wants to know where farmers have risen up and formed a serious protest movement, it started in Mallee, and I am very proud of those farmers. They're there to farm. That's what they want to do. It is the most important thing to them. It has been the most important thing to their grandparents and their great-grandparents, and so I could go on. Sixth- and seventh-generation farmers are now finding it so hard to farm under this government. It's not only the red tape, the green tape and all the biosecurity issues they now have to worry about. We've got carbon tax. We now have renewable energy rolling through their properties and forced acquisitions by the Victorian Labor government. But lo and behold, today we find that the Victorian Premier has made the announcement that the Western Renewables Link is going to go into

speaker: Renee Coffey
heading: MATTERS OF PUBLIC IMPORTANCE · Energy
text: Last Sunday, in my community in West End at the Kurilpa Derby, I had many conversations about the future that people want for our community, and I'll give a big shout-out to Moira, who had a very long chat with me. What I heard, time and again, is that people in my community want ambitious climate action and a clean energy transition that lowers household bills. They also want renters to share in those savings. They expect their government to listen, lead and deliver. As the only progressive party in Australia that can form a government, we know we must lead that debate and also deliver environmental and energy policy. That responsibility belongs to Labor, and it is only Labor that rises to that challenge. Addressing climate change is a moral imperative, is an economic imperative and is what my community wants. Earlier this month we heard some distressing news. For more than a decade the world has been working towards limiting global warming to 1.5 degrees. The United Nations

speaker: Renee Coffey
heading: MATTERS OF PUBLIC IMPORTANCE · Energy
text: Environment Programme has warned that we will very likely exceed that threshold within this decade. Avoiding an overshoot is no longer a realistic prospect. This is devastating news, particularly for our Pacific island neighbours facing rising seas and threats to their homes. We cannot pretend that climate change isn't real. We cannot ignore it, and we cannot give up and say it is all too hard. Climate change is part of our lives. We must adapt and limit the worst of its effects. Every fraction of a degree we prevent reduces harm. Failing to seize the opportunities of a clean economy would work against Australia's national interests, particularly the interests of those that come after us. I am proud to be part of a Labor government that is rising to that challenge. More than 44 per cent of homes in Griffith have solar panels. Our community is already helping build a cleaner electricity system. Complementing rooftop solar, home batteries let households store electricity generated during the day and use it

speaker: Renee Coffey
heading: MATTERS OF PUBLIC IMPORTANCE · Energy
text: after sunset when families are cooking dinner and switching on appliances. I was proud that our government announced the Cheaper Home Batteries Program, right in my community, last year—a program that reduces the cost of a typical battery around 30 per cent. Since 1 July last year, it has supported more than 500,000 battery installations for households, small businesses and community groups. Griffith has recorded 2,258 solar batteries, providing more than 68,000 kilowatt hours of usable storage. It's a shame that the member for Wannon has left because in his electorate they have installed 2,253 cheaper home batteries. He's just five short of mine—catching up!—but I've got no doubt that they will get there very soon. We have expanded that program to support an expected two million installations by 2030. For renters, access to benefits requires government actions. A tenant can face high electricity bills without having any control over the roof above them. The Solar Sharer Offer gives eligible households the option of three hours of free electricity usage

speaker: Renee Coffey
heading: MATTERS OF PUBLIC IMPORTANCE · Energy
text: in the middle of the day. Our Community Solar Banks program has delivered solar installations for more than 5,200 apartments, with renters occupying almost half. We are also investing more than $20 billion through Rewiring the Nation to modernise the grid. Another 15 large battery projects selected through our Capacity Investment Scheme are expected to attract around $6 billion in private investment. These projects will support more than 6,800 jobs across construction, operations and maintenance. Australians are changing how they get around, too. Last month, battery electric vehicles outsold petrol vehicles for the first time, becoming the largest single fuel category in new vehicle sales—more than 27,000 sold in August—accounting for almost a quarter of the market. This is electrification in practice; more Australians are replacing petrol with electricity, reducing their reliance on fossil fuels and cutting their running costs. It's a bit rich for those opposite to talk about failing energy policy. They spent years in government unable to settle on a lasting policy of their own—and then they

speaker: Renee Coffey
heading: MATTERS OF PUBLIC IMPORTANCE · Energy
text: came up with nuclear. Now the coalition is chasing One Nation and retreating further from the climate action that Australians need. Look at what One Nation senator Malcolm Roberts is saying. At a Senate hearing just this year, he claimed: There is no data at all that shows there's a changing climate, only inherent natural variation in cycles. He's promoted claims of a UN-inspired climate hoax and accused the Bureau of Meteorology of interfering with climate data. Climate change isn't a debate; it is our reality. In my community of Griffith, people tell me every day they want action, not excuses. The Albanese Labor government is showing leadership, setting strong climate targets, investing in renewables and driving down emissions while creating local jobs. That's progress, not politics.

speaker: Tony Pasin
heading: MATTERS OF PUBLIC IMPORTANCE · Energy
text: To any steelworkers from Whyalla who might have just been listening to that contribution, that was the member for Griffith. Where is Griffith? Griffith is an affluent inner-city electorate in Brisbane, along the Brisbane River—certainly no steelworkers, or very few, I would hasten to suggest. Unfortunately, what they would have heard was not what they wanted to hear. What they wanted to hear was the once proud Labor Party standing up for them, their industry and their jobs. Instead, what they heard was, 'You're just a casualty of the ideological war we're perpetrating on the Australian people.' That's what they heard—the once-proud Labor Party who stood up for workers now turns their back on workers. These may well be workers in regional South Australia—and that might not matter to you—but it matters to me. It's not in my electorate, but it's significant. The other thing that matters to me is that—in a country where we export phenomenal amounts of coking coal, where we have available to us phenomenal amounts of coking coal and where we have iron ore exports that rival the rest of the world—we will no longer produce structural steel. We have flown the white flag on the capacity to build or create steel.

speaker: Tony Pasin
heading: MATTERS OF PUBLIC IMPORTANCE · Energy
text: The member for McEwen says, 'You have.' I would never suggest, Madam Deputy Speaker, that in the chair you would do such a thing. But the truth is that those opposite have done this. And how have you done it? You've done it by pursuing this ideological renewables-only agenda, which has driven up the price of electricity. During question time, we heard from those opposite seeking to blame the former owner of the steel mill, Mr Gupta, about his failure to undertake maintenance on the blast furnace. This was a situation where, quite frankly, in the state that experiences the highest electricity costs in Australia and in turn potentially the highest electricity costs in the world—and again, who do we have to blame for that? It's an agenda that is driven by those opposite, who want to drive up the cost of electricity not just for households but for businesses. We shouldn't be surprised—should we—that the businesses most likely to fail in that setting are those businesses that rely heavily on electricity and the cost of energy. Those really energy-intensive industries are going to fail first.

speaker: Tony Pasin
heading: MATTERS OF PUBLIC IMPORTANCE · Energy
text: I seem to encourage interest from those opposite, and I'm pleased. Because—through you, Madam Deputy Speaker—I suggest to the House that, as a result of this really difficult decision that was delivered to 500 or 600 South Australian regional workers by the Premier of South Australia yesterday, there won't be any less structural steel utilised globally or indeed in Australia. But now it'll be produced in jurisdictions who care less about carbon emissions, who care less about workers' safety, who care less about workers and what workers are paid. I want to live in an Australia that makes things. I want to live in an Australia where we don't have the working poor. As the brother of a dead worker who died on the job, I want to make sure people making things can do it safely, but unfortunately those opposite want to live in this utopia where unfortunately you can drive up the cost of energy but heavy industry survives in Australia. It isn't exposed to global competition. That's exactly what's happening. speaker: Sarah Witty
heading: MATTERS OF PUBLIC IMPORTANCE · Energy
text: For years, everyday Australians watched the other political parties in this place turn energy into a political battleground rather than a responsibility. One side spent a decade denying reality. The other confused protests with progress, slogans with solutions. They created outrage but instead of doing something about it turned that outrage into data harvesting personal information for their own political gain. In the middle are everyday families and businesses who just want affordable energy, reliable power and confidence that climate change is being taken seriously. Australia's energy system was always going to change. Our coal-fired power stations are getting older. The question has never been whether the transition would happen. The question has been whether Australia would be prepared for it. For 10 years those opposite had the opportunity to prepare. What did they deliver? It was a promise of wholesale prices below $70 per megawatt hour but with a reality of prices above $280. It was 10 years in government, 10 years of climate wars and 10 years where

speaker: Sarah Witty

speaker: Zali Steggall
heading: STATEMENTS BY MEMBERS · Climate Change
text: Today's events in parliament underline the biggest threat to our way of life and our safety: global warming. Communities on the front line of extreme weather are already paying the price. The most vulnerable often have the fewest resources to prepare, recover or escape mounting disasters. Doctors for the Environment Australia are here sounding the alarm on gas: its contribution to global warming, how it's accelerating heating and the health risks from burning it in our homes, including the rising rates of childhood asthma. Uniting Care Australia are here briefing us on the impacts of extreme weather and the impacts to vulnerable communities. Yet this government recklessly continues supporting and approving gas and fossil fuel expansion. Today's Australian built showcase demonstrates the alternative: renewable investment and Australian technology that can cut emissions, lower bills, create jobs and build prosperity. The international context matters. Tuvalu's climate change minister is also here today, building consensus for stronger action ahead of pre-COP. For our Pacific neighbours, climate action is a matter of survival. Whilst the Australian government makes a lot of promises and well-meaning statements, its actions do not match that. speaker: Dan Tehan
heading: BILLS · Carbon Credits and Other Legislation Amendment (Integrity and Transparency) Bill 2026; Second Reading
text: The Carbon Credits and Other Legislation Amendment (Integrity and Transparency) Bill 2026 is significant, complex and cannot be supported. On its face, it purports to make a series of technical changes to the operation of Australia's $50 billion carbon credits market, but, like every piece of legislation that this Albanese Labor government puts in place, it's got an ideological underpinning to it which is going to do harm. And, as I will explain, this piece of legislation is no different to all the other pieces of legislation which the Albanese Labor government has put in place when it comes to their ideologically driven net zero agenda. With some exceptions, these changes are mostly uncontroversial. They include a new incentive structure for the role of R&D in carbon abatement, the establishment of a new oversight body, shifting certain powers from the Clean Energy Regulator to the Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water. But, as I have said, this bill is a wolf in sheep's clothing. I'll be very

speaker: Dan Tehan
heading: BILLS · Carbon Credits and Other Legislation Amendment (Integrity and Transparency) Bill 2026; Second Reading
text: clear at the outset. The coalition will oppose this fundamentally flawed and regressive net zero bill. Had the bill been limited to the changes that I mentioned earlier, then it would have stood a better chance of attracting support from the coalition. After all, the coalition does support an effective and robust carbon credit market that helps Australian companies reduce their emissions responsibly and competitively, but this bill goes way beyond making a few administrative-in-nature changes. The bill greatly expands Australia's native title regime, removes the least-cost financial test and hands the minister sweeping new carbon credit powers. As I will explain in detail, these are deeply consequential amendments that the coalition cannot support. Australia's carbon credits market, formally the Australian Carbon Credit Unit Scheme, has been operating in Australia since 2011. It has operated under successive governments, albeit under extremely different rules, policy objectives and names. At its core, however, its intent has remained the same: (a) to support companies to reduce their emissions from industrial processes and (b)

speaker: Dan Tehan
heading: BILLS · Carbon Credits and Other Legislation Amendment (Integrity and Transparency) Bill 2026; Second Reading
text: to back emissions sequestration, that is, storing carbon in vegetation or soil. As it currently operates, companies can use the scheme to implement eligible emissions reduction projects using approved methods and earn one Australian carbon credit unit for each tonne of carbon dioxide equivalent emissions that the project avoids or stores. Participants can then sell ACCUs to the Australian government by entering into a carbon abatement contract or to private entities who need to surrender ACCUs to meet compliance obligations under the safeguard mechanism. Labor changed the safeguard mechanism in mid-2023. Under this change, baselines for emissions reductions were adjusted so that they sharply decline. Consequentially, a company which exceeds its baselines must purchase carbon credits to offset their emissions. I remind members, again, that the coalition does not support Labor's punitive safeguard mechanism, which is a carbon tax. We want to abolish it. One of the principal concerns that the coalition has with this bill is the changes to the native title arrangements. Currently, the Carbon Credits (Carbon Farming

speaker: Dan Tehan
heading: BILLS · Carbon Credits and Other Legislation Amendment (Integrity and Transparency) Bill 2026; Second Reading
text: Initiative) Act 2011 provides for the conditional registration of eligible offset projects on native title land before the consent of eligible interest holders has been obtained. In practice, this means that any project may be established for up to five years—the first reporting period—before it is required to provide evidence to the Clean Energy Regulator that eligible interest holders' consent has been obtained to undertake that project. The bill, in sections 27 and 28, dramatically upends this process. The bill establishes that a mere claim to native title would become an eligible interest. Accordingly, this would require someone wanting to establish a carbon abatement project to deal with a claim to native title, regardless as to whether the title actually exists or exists at law. That is a monumental change and, as a precedent, would have monumental consequences. This new approval process is part of a more cumbersome two-stage consent process for setting up a carbon abatement project. Among other things, the Clean Energy Regulator, at section 32, would be

speaker: Dan Tehan
heading: BILLS · Carbon Credits and Other Legislation Amendment (Integrity and Transparency) Bill 2026; Second Reading
text: the proposed change actually fixing? Under the current carbon credit regime, native title holders enjoy absolute, rock-solid legal protections. These include that a project proponent must obtain the consent of the native title holder, and there is a built-in right to negotiate. Secondly, this change goes beyond what the government's own report recommended. So, once again, I do question why the government is doing this when its own report didn't recommend it. In introducing this bill, the assistant minister asserted that the changes this bill is trying to make arise from the 2022 Chubb review. This simply isn't the case. I don't know what's happening to this government, but I fear, under the Prime Minister's leadership, that they're learning to just make things up and think, if they just say it, it's true. Well, there are actual facts that matter. And the Prime Minister mightn't like that. He mightn't like the fact it seems he's given Rhys Muldoon a reference. But, if he has, it's a fact. And you've got

speaker: Dan Tehan
heading: BILLS · Carbon Credits and Other Legislation Amendment (Integrity and Transparency) Bill 2026; Second Reading
text: holders but also Native Title claimants. The legal realities of expanding the native title regime are unclear at best. As a matter of fact, I think you're going to make things so much worse it's not funny. It's funny, when we had the departmental briefing and we asked questions about this, no-one could see that this would do anything else but make the regime more complex. According to the Indigenous Carbon Industry Network, who support this bill and have met personally with the assistant minister, 11 per cent of Australia's landmass is currently under a native title claim, awaiting a decision to be made by the Federal Court as to the area's native title status. Thirdly, these changes throw up a range of complicated logistical questions for project proponents. In their submission to the prior consultation process on this bill, the National Farmers' Federation recommended the government replace the regime proposed in this bill and instead opt for a right-to-negotiate-style process similar to that applied under the future acts regime.

speaker: Dan Tehan
heading: BILLS · Carbon Credits and Other Legislation Amendment (Integrity and Transparency) Bill 2026; Second Reading
text: The NFF's evidence is particularly compelling. They found that negotiations underway under the current regime are already too difficult, too protracted and not conducted in good faith. For example, they point to reports of landholders having to pay money upfront simply for an initial sit-down meeting with an eligible interest holder. Worryingly, the NFF states that such events are not isolated but rather reflect a pattern of behaviour experienced by the sector nationwide. The NFF's position that the ACCU scheme should not convert a prospective claim that has not yet been formally determined into an indefinite consent right is strongly made and strongly backed by the coalition. The NFF is not alone in raising concerns about the proposed expansion of native title. AgForce Queensland, which represents 6,000 farmers who manage a combined 55 million hectares of land, argue that the proposed changes 'risk creating substantial uncertainty' which 'significantly increase project establishment costs, transaction complexity and delays for agricultural producers'. The energy industry has also raised concerns about the practical application

speaker: Dan Tehan
heading: BILLS · Carbon Credits and Other Legislation Amendment (Integrity and Transparency) Bill 2026; Second Reading
text: of these changes. Woodside Energy has similarly raised concerns with the government's proposal, stating that the change may cause investment uncertainty which may reduce and delay ACCU supply. While expressing in-principle support for generally strengthening Australia's native title regime, AGL Energy have advised the government of issues around implementation. AGL have sought advice on how overlapping or competing claims to native titles would be resolved. Importantly, AGL have sought additional advice from the government as to how this native title expansion would support sufficient consent processes while at the same time maintaining timely project delivery. Thank you, Member for Groom. Finally, the Business Council of Australia has also raised concerns around the proposed native title expansion. The BCA have warned of unintended consequences with the proposed changes, stating that the bill ought to include 'specific guidelines for clear evidence requirements, standard forms of service level timeframes to minimise registration delays and uncertainty in the consent process'. The opposition is concerned that expanding native title in this way would unleash more

speaker: Dan Tehan

In effect, the act requires the government to

speaker: Dan Tehan

text: the view that: (1) the bill: (a) progresses the Government's failing net zero agenda; (b) increases lawfare, undermines responsible emissions reduction, and raises costs on industry; (c) repeals the 'least cost' test in favour of an opaque 'value for money' regime; and (d) hands the Minister for Climate Change and Energy new, unilateral powers on an unfounded basis; (2) the Government's deal in the Senate on Thursday, 10 September 2026, undermines the integrity of the Australian Carbon Credit Units Scheme; and (3) the Government must scrap its punitive carbon tax, the Safeguard Mechanism". Something is always afoot when the coalition and the Greens hold nearly identical positions on bills. heading: BILLS · Carbon Credits and Other Legislation Amendment (Integrity and Transparency) Bill 2026; Second Reading

It means that the minister can interfere with projects that have already been put in place by landholders, to be able to access ACCUs. So, once again, I just sit here and think, 'Who dreamt this up?'
